李植〔貫山西大同府大同縣民籍，府學生，治《易經》，字汝培，行二，年二十六，五月初十日生〕。曾祖英；祖滿〔贈奉政大夫、兵部郎中〕；父承式〔布政司左叅政〕；母郭氏〔贈宜人〕；繼母閆氏〔封宜人〕。具慶下。兄模；弟梃、楨、槓、栱、杜、樹、楫、枝、樟。娶蔣氏。山西鄉試第二十名，會試第一百八十一名。
translation_en:
Li Zaiyang 李載陽 [registered in a military household in Qizhou 蘄州, Huangzhou Prefecture 黃州府, Huguang 湖廣; a Department Student (zhouxuesheng) specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Zichun 子春; first in seniority among his brothers; aged twenty-eight, born on the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month]. His great-grandfather was Li Bai 李栢; his grandfather was Li Shiyan 李時言 [Department Magistrate (zhizhou), promoted in prestige title to Grand Master exemplar (zhongxian dafu)]; his father is Li Yuanying 李元英; his mother was née Jiang 姜氏; and his stepmother is née Deng 鄧氏. Both his grandparents and parents are living. His younger brothers are Li Chengyang 李承陽, Li Yingyang 李應陽, Li Deyang 李得陽, and Li Taiyang 李泰陽. He married née Hua 化氏. He placed twentieth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and two hundred eighteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Mengri 趙夢日 [registered in Guiji County 會稽縣, native of Shanyin County 山陰縣, Shaoxing Prefecture 紹興府, Zhejiang 浙江; a Student of the Directorate of Education (guozisheng) specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Yingrui 應瑞; fourteenth in seniority among his brothers and cousins; aged thirty-three, born on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month]. His great-grandfather was Zhao Qi 趙祺 [Honorary Official of the Seventh Rank (qipin sanguan)]; his grandfather was Zhao Pu 趙溥; his father is Zhao Tang 趙棠; and his mother is née Zhou 周氏. Both his parents are living. His elder brothers are Zhao Mengfeng 趙夢鳳 [District Magistrate (zhixian)], Zhao Wan 趙完 [Assistant Prefect (tongpan)], Zhao Mengba 趙夢罷 [?], and Zhao Mengyuan 趙夢鵷 [Student of the Directorate of Education (jiansheng)]; his younger brothers are Zhao Menghong 趙夢鴻, Zhao Menglei 趙夢雷, Zhao Mengdou 趙夢斗, Zhao Meng'e 趙夢鶚, and Zhao Mengkui 趙夢魁. He married née Xia 夏氏. He placed tenth in the Shuntian Prefecture 順天府 Provincial Examination and two hundred thirty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lian Ge 連格 [registered in a military household in Yuzhou 禹州, Kaifeng Prefecture 開封府, Henan 河南; a Student of the Directorate of Education (guozisheng) specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing); courtesy name Mengshi 孟式; first in seniority among his brothers; aged forty, born on the seventeenth day of the first month]. His great-grandfather was Lian Ang 連昂; his grandfather was Lian Ji 連吉 [District Jailor (dianshi)]; his father was Lian Pan 連泮; and his mother was née Li 李氏. Both his parents are deceased. His younger brother is Lian Biao 連標. He married née Zhang 張氏, and successively remarried née Zhang 張氏 and née Wang 王氏. He placed twenty-first in the Henan Provincial Examination and one hundred sixty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Zhi 李植 [registered in a civilian household in Datong County 大同縣, Datong Prefecture 大同府, Shanxi 山西; a Prefectural Student (fuxuesheng) specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Rupei 汝培; second in seniority among his brothers; aged twenty-six, born on the tenth day of the fifth month]. His great-grandfather was Li Ying 李英; his grandfather was Li Man 李滿 [posthumously honored as Grand Master for Governance (fengzheng dafu) and Director of a Bureau in the Ministry of War (bingbu langzhong)]; his father is Li Chengshi 李承式 [Left Administration Vice Commissioner (buzhengsi zuo canzheng)]; his mother was née Guo 郭氏 [posthumously honored as Lady of Suitability (yiren)]; and his stepmother is née Yan 閆氏 [invested as Lady of Suitability (yiren)]. Both his father and stepmother are living. His elder brother is Li Mo 李模; his younger brothers are Li Ting 李梃, Li Zhen 李楨, Li Gang 李槓, Li Gong 李栱, Li Du 李杜, Li Shu 李樹, Li Ji 李楫, Li Zhi 李枝, and Li Zhang 李樟. He married née Jiang 蔣氏. He placed twentieth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and one hundred eighty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Dengyun 陳登雲 (registered in a civilian household of Tangshan County, Shunde Prefecture, Southern Metropolitan Area [Zhili]; a County Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry; style name Conglong; seniority first; age twenty-eight, born on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month). His great-grandfather was Zhongliang; his grandfather was Ao; his father is Zhida; his father's first wife was née Li, and his mother is née Shi. Both parents are living. He married née Zhang. He placed 60th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 80th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Weixin 張維新 (registered in a military household of Ruzhou, Henan; a Subprefectural Student; specialized in the Classic of Changes; style name Xianzhou; seniority first; age twenty-eight, born on the eighth day of the sixth month). His great-grandfather was Keyong (Subprefectural Judge); his grandfather was Cui (tribute student [gongshi]); his father is Congyi (Confucian Official by grace regulation); his mother is née Ding. Both parents are living. His elder cousins/brothers are Weijing and Weicong; his younger brothers are Weizhen, Weiyun, and Weiyang. He married née Qi, and subsequently married née Shi. He placed 28th in the Henan Provincial Examination and 270th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Jie 陸玠 (registered in a civilian household of Hejiang County, Luzhou, Sichuan; a National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Changes; style name Zhongyu; seniority second; age thirty-three, born on the twenty-fourth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Yongtai; his grandfather was Chong; his father was Cunhuan; his father's first wife was née Tao, and his mother is née Wang. His mother is living. His elder brother is Tang; his younger brother is Rui. He married née Zhang. He placed 29th in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 289th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fang Wanshan 方萬山 (registered in a civilian household of She County, Huizhou Prefecture, Southern Metropolitan Area [Zhili]; a National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Changes; style name Yangzhi; seniority first; age thirty-one, born on the second day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Congdao; his grandfather was Qi; his father is Rizhang; his mother is née Wu. Both parents are living. His younger brothers are Wanchuan, Wansong, and Wanshun. He married née Xu. He placed 56th in the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 59th in the Metropolitan Examination.

葉祖堯〔貫雲南臨安衛官籍，直隸鳳陽府鳳陽縣人，國子生，治《易經》，字允中，行一，年二十六，九月初二日生〕。曾祖聰〔學正，贈主事〕；祖瑞〔戶部主事〕；父之美〔訓導〕；母濮氏。嚴侍下。弟祖舜、祖禹、祖文、祖武、祖履、祖臯。娶馮氏。雲南鄉試第三十二名，會試第一百九十名。
translation_en:
Chen Jian 陳簡 [registered in a civilian household of Tunliu County, Lu'an Prefecture, Shanxi; Student of the Directorate of Education; specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Jujing; third in his generation; age twenty-seven; born on the third day of the eighth month]. His great-grandfather was Chen Fu; his grandfather was Chen Cang; his father is Chen Shifeng [Prefectural Assistant Prefect]; his mother is Lady Li. Both of his parents are living. His elder brothers are Chen Fan and Chen Ce. He married Lady Jin. He placed forty-eighth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and one hundred fifty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tian Yilin 田一麟 [registered in an artisan household of Xiangfu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan; Prefectural Student; specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Daozheng; first in his generation; age twenty-five; born on the twenty-ninth day of the first month]. His great-grandfather was Tian An [Assistant Magistrate, posthumously granted the title of Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Justice]; his grandfather was Tian Ruzi [Office Manager in the Ministry of War]; his father is Tian Longyao; his mother is Lady Jia. Both of his parents are living. His younger brothers are Tian Yifeng [tribute student (gongshi)], Tian Yihe, and Tian Yipeng. He married Lady Zhang. He placed forty-fourth in the Henan Provincial Examination and two hundred third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Jiuchou 陳九疇 [registered in a civilian household of Licheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong; Student of the Directorate of Education; specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Shixu; first in his generation; age forty-two; born on the fourth day of the tenth month]. His great-grandfather was Chen Lin; his grandfather was Chen Zi; his father was Chen Zhong; his mother was Lady Zhang. Both of his parents are deceased. His younger brother is Chen Jiugong. He married Lady Qi. He placed second in the Shandong Provincial Examination and two hundred ninety-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ye Zuyao 葉祖堯 [registered in an official household of Lin'an Guard, Yunnan, originally from Fengyang County, Fengyang Prefecture, Southern Metropolitan Area (Zhili); Student of the Directorate of Education; specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Yunzhong; first in his generation; age twenty-six; born on the second day of the ninth month]. His great-grandfather was Ye Cong [Subprefectural Instructor, posthumously granted the title of Secretary]; his grandfather was Ye Rui [Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue]; his father is Ye Zhimei [Assistant Instructor]; his mother was Lady Pu. His father is living and his mother is deceased. His younger brothers are Ye Zushun, Ye Zuyu, Ye Zuwen, Ye Zuwu, Ye Zulü, and Ye Zugao. He married Lady Feng. He placed thirty-second in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and one hundred ninetieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Sun Xuan 孫玄 (courtesy name Shuqian 叔乾, first in seniority) was registered in a civilian household in Dongping Subprefecture 東平州, Yanzhou Prefecture 兗州府, Shandong 山東. A National University Student (國子生) specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing 詩經), he was thirty-five sui, born on the twelfth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Sun Kui 逵, a District Magistrate (知縣); his grandfather was Sun Fengzong 奉宗, holding prestige title without functional assignment (散官); his father was Sun Cunyi 存義, a Subprefectural Magistrate (知州); and his mother was née Li 李氏. Both his parents and grandparents were living (重慶下). He married a woman née Gong 鞏氏. He placed 19th in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 205th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Jiuguan 陳九官 (courtesy name Zhongfu 忠甫, fourth in seniority) was registered in a military household in Yin County 鄞縣, Ningbo Prefecture 寧波府, Zhejiang 浙江. A National University Student specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing 易經), he was thirty-three sui, born on the fourteenth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Chen Yi 益; his grandfather was Chen Da 達; his father was Chen Wu 武; and his mother was née Lin 林氏. His father was living and his mother was deceased (嚴侍下). He had an elder brother, Chen Zong 宗, and younger brothers, Chen Jiude 九德, Chen Jiugong 九功, and Chen Jiusi 九思. He married a woman née Zhuang 莊氏. He placed 28th in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 195th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yixin 張一心 (courtesy name Daozong 道宗, second in seniority) was registered in a civilian household in Huolu County 獲鹿縣, Zhending Prefecture 真定府, Zhili 直隸. A National University Student specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing 易經), he was thirty-one sui, born on the twenty-third day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Zhang Sen 森; his grandfather was Zhang Pan 磐; his father was Zhang Yinghui 楹惠; his mother was née Du 杜氏; and his stepmother was née Li 李氏. His father was living and his mothers were deceased (嚴侍下). He had an elder brother, Zhang Yiguan 一貫, and younger brothers, Zhang Daye 大冶 and Zhang Sicong 四聰. He married a woman née Feng 馮氏. He placed 131st in the Shuntian Prefecture 順天府 Provincial Examination and 227th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Xiangchun 萬象春 (courtesy name Renfu 仁甫, first in seniority) was registered in a civilian household in Wuxi County 無錫縣, Changzhou Prefecture 常州府, Zhili 直隸. A National University Student specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing 書經), he was twenty-six sui, born on the twenty-fifth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Wan Kai 愷; his grandfather was Wan He 和; his father was Wan Tianxiang 天祥; and his mother was née Zhou 周氏. Both his parents were living (具慶下). He had younger brothers, Wan Xiangxin 象新 and Wan Xiangming 象明. He married a woman née Su 蘇氏. He placed 121st in the Yingtian Prefecture 應天府 Provincial Examination and 44th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Daixing 吳道行 (registered under a military household in Binzhou 濱州, Jinan Prefecture 濟南府, Shandong; National University Student; specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals [Chunqiu]; courtesy name Mingshi 名世; first in generational seniority; aged thirty-five, born on the second day of the third month). His great-grandfather was Wu Guan 瓘 (Assistant District Magistrate); his grandfather was Wu Yi 宜 (District Director of Schools); his father is Wu Shijin 士進 (Honorary Elder), his mother was née Cheng 成, and his stepmother is née Shang 尚. His father is living. He has a younger brother, Daoji 道濟. He married née Zheng 鄭. He placed thirty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and two hundred ninety-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Yingtu 馬應圖 (registered under a civilian household in Pinghu County 平湖縣, Jiaxing Prefecture 嘉興府, Zhejiang; National University Student; specialized in the Book of Documents [Shujing]; courtesy name Xinyi 心易; first in generational seniority; aged thirty, born on the twenty-second day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Ma Sheng 昇 (Prefectural Administrative Clerk); his grandfather was Ma Ke 珂 (District Director of Schools); his father is Ma Shicheng 師程 (Confucian Official by Special Grace), his mother was née Huang 黃, and his stepmother is née Shen 沈. Both his parents are living. He has a younger brother, Taitu 泰圖. He married née Tu 屠. He placed second in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and two hundred seventy-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Keli 羊可立 (registered under a military household in the Qunmu Battalion 羣牧所, Runing Prefecture 汝寧府, Henan, a native of Ruyang County 汝陽縣; National University Student; specialized in the Book of Odes [Shijing]; courtesy name Ziyu 子豫; first in generational seniority; aged twenty-eight, born on the second day of the twelfth month). His great-grandfather was Yang You 友; his grandfather was Yang Wenqing 文慶 (Honorary Elder); his father was Yang Jie 傑 (District Magistrate), his father's former wives were née Fang 方 and née Yuan 苑, and his mother was née Sheng 盛. Both his parents are deceased. He has younger brothers, Kejiu 可久, Keyou 可由, Ke'ai 可愛, and Keshi 可仕. He married née Zhang 張. He placed fifty-fifth in the Henan Provincial Examination and one hundred seventy-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Huaishu 劉懷恕 (registered under a civilian household in Dongming County 東明縣, Daming Prefecture 大名府, Zhili; National University Student; specialized in the Book of Odes [Shijing]; courtesy name Shixing 士行; third in generational seniority; aged twenty-eight, born on the tenth day of the ninth month). His great-grandfather was Liu Jun 俊; his grandfather was Liu Yi 儀; his father is Liu Tianxiang 天祥, and his mother is née Zhang 張. Both his parents are living. He has elder brothers, Huai'en 懷恩 and Huaihui 懷惠, and younger brothers, Huaizhi 懷志, Huaixian 懷憲, and Huaici 懷慈. He married née Zhang 張, and subsequently married née Zhao 趙 and née Tao 陶. He placed one hundred thirty-eighth in the Shuntian Prefecture 順天府 Provincial Examination and two hundred twentieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Yuan Yikui 原一魁 is registered under a military household in Ye County 掖縣, Laizhou Prefecture 萊州府, Shandong 山東. He is a prefectural student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), with the courtesy name Zhongwen 仲文; he is the second in seniority among his brothers, thirty-five years old, and was born on the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Yuan Xu 旭; his grandfather was Yuan Run 潤; his father was Yuan Siqing 思慶; his legal mother was Lady Xu 徐氏, and his birth mother is Lady Zhang 張氏. His mother is still living. His elder brother is Yuan Yili 一理 (Assistant Magistrate), and his younger brother is Yuan Yixing 一性. He married Lady Teng 滕氏. He placed twenty-eighth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and two hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jing Zhoutu 荆州土 is registered under a military household in Linjin County 臨晉縣, Puzhou 蒲州, Pingyang Prefecture 平陽府, Shanxi 山西. He is a student of the Directorate of Education (Guozisheng) specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), with the courtesy name Zhiyuan 至元; he is the first in seniority among his brothers, thirty-five years old, and was born on the sixth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jing Feng 鳳; his grandfather was Jing Daxue 大學; his father is Jing Chunfang 春芳; and his mother is Lady Yang 楊氏. Both of his parents are still living. His younger brothers are Jing Zhoujin 州金 and Jing Zhoutian 州田. He married Lady Bai 白氏. He placed twenty-sixth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and two hundred eleventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Jin 魯錦 is registered under a military household in Shanyin County 山陰縣, Shaoxing Prefecture 紹興府, Zhejiang 浙江. He is a [four illegible characters] specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), with the courtesy name Wenshu 文叔; he is the second in seniority among his brothers, thirty-one years old, and was born on the eighth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Lu Yan 儼; his grandfather was Lu Dazhong 大中; his father was Lu Zongcheng 宗程; his mother was Lady Wu 吳氏, and his stepmother was Lady Liang 梁氏. Both of his parents are deceased. His elder brother is Lu Qin 欽, and his younger brothers are Lu Lian 鐮, Lu Hao 鎬, Lu Zheng 鉦, Lu Yao 鑰, Lu Xi 錫, Lu Chong 銃, Lu Rong 鎔, and Lu Qi 錡. He married Lady Hu 胡氏. He placed eighty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Hechun 杜和春 is registered under a military household in Longxi County 隴西縣, Gongchang Prefecture 鞏昌府, Shaanxi 陝西. He is a student of the Directorate of Education (Guozisheng) specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing), with the courtesy name Tijian 體健; he is the second in seniority among his brothers, twenty-eight years old, and was born on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Du Zong 總 (Honorary Official of Advanced Age); his grandfather was Du Wenqing 文清; his father is Du Xin 心; and his mother is Lady Huo 霍氏. Both of his parents are still living. His elder brother is Du Xiangchun 向春, and his younger brothers are Du Yuchun 遇春, Du Changchun 長春, Du Yingchun 迎春, and Du Rongchun 榮春. He married Lady Sun 孫氏, and subsequently married Lady Liu 劉氏. He placed forty-third in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and two hundred ninetieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Gan Shijia 甘士价 (registered in a civilian household of Xinfeng County, Ganzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Weifan; fifth in seniority among his generation; age twenty-five, born on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month). His great-grandfather was Gan Ruizhen; his grandfather was Gan Gong; his father is Gan Wenbing; and his mother is née Wu. Both of his parents are living. His elder brothers are Gan Shijie, Gan Shiyang, Gan Shizuo, and Gan Shiyi; his younger brothers are Gan Shilun and Gan Shiquan. He married née Wu. He placed twenty-second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 194th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Shixu 沈時叙 (registered in a physician household of Xiangfu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Gongna; first in seniority among his generation; age thirty, born on the sixth day of the seventh month). His great-grandfather was Shen Zhen (Reader-companion in a Princely Establishment); his grandfather was Shen Xiang; his father was Shen Zhaofan (Tribute Student [gongshi]); his mother was née Li; and his stepmother is née Lü. His mother (stepmother) is living, while his father is deceased. His younger brother is Shen Shibao. He married née Li. He placed thirtieth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 245th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qu Qianqiao 曲遷喬 (registered in a civilian household of Changshan County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Documents [Shujing]; courtesy name Yunsheng; first in seniority among his generation; age thirty, born on the fifth day of the fifth month). His great-grandfather was Qu Hui; his grandfather is Qu Huan; his father is Qu Lai; and his mother is née Xu. Both his parents and grandparents are living. His younger brothers are Qu Qianshan, Qu Qianwu, and Qu Qianzhong. He married née Wang. He placed 104th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 201st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tan Gui 譚桂 (registered in a civilian household of Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Changes [Yijing]; courtesy name Shifang; fourth in seniority among his generation; age thirty-two, born on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month). His great-grandfather was Tan Guangcheng; his grandfather was Tan Hu; his father was Tan Xun (granted an honorary cap and belt by grace); and his mother is née Wan. His mother is living, while his father is deceased. His elder brothers are Tan Yueyong, Tan Yuejia, and Tan Yueyao; his younger brothers are Tan Yuefu and Tan Yuekui. He married née Wu. He placed fifteenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 186th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Fei Shangyi 費尚伊 (registered in a military household of Mianyang Subprefecture, Chengtian Prefecture, Huguang; Student of the Directorate of Education; specialized in the Classic of Documents [Shujing]; courtesy name Guoping; fifth in seniority; aged twenty-four; born on the nineteenth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Fei Jun; his grandfather was Fei Hua; his father was Fei Dezhi (tribute student [gongshi]); his mother was née Chen, and his stepmother is née Ren. Both parents are living. His elder brothers are Shangzhong, Shangwen, and Shangyou; his younger brothers are Shangkui, Shangda, Shangzhou, Shanglü, and Shangji. He married née Se, and remarried née Zhang. He placed eighteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and one hundred and ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ning Hualong 甯化龍 (registered in a civilian household of Xin'an County, An Subprefecture, Baoding Prefecture, Zhili; County Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Wenming; second in seniority; aged twenty-six; born on the first day of the twelfth month). His great-grandfather was Ning Hai; his grandfather is Ning Zhiben; his father is Ning Jie (Prestige Official [sanguan]); his mother is née Wu. Both his parents and grandparents are living. His elder brother is Yuelong, and his younger brothers are Yunlong and Panlong. He married née Wang, and remarried née Yang. He placed seventy-second in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and two hundred and forty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Wenzi 吳文梓 (registered in a civilian household of Qingyang County, Chizhou Prefecture, Zhili; Student of the Directorate of Education; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Ziqiao; second in seniority; aged thirty; born on the twelfth day of the seventh month). His great-grandfather was Wu Zongli; his grandfather was Wu Jingqing; his father is Wu Shifan; his mother is née Ke. Both parents are living. His elder brother is Wenxian, and his younger brothers are Wennan (Directorate Student [jiansheng]), Wenlin (Directorate Student [jiansheng]), Wenyuan, Wenjing (Directorate Student [jiansheng]), Wenshi, and Wenwei. He married née Jiang, and remarried née Ye. He placed thirty-third in the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination and two hundred and forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Jing 張敬 (registered in a civilian household of Zichuan County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong; Student of the Directorate of Education; specialized in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Erhe; first in seniority; aged thirty-five; born on the fifth day of the eighth month). His great-grandfather was Zhang Xian; his grandfather was Zhang Quan; his father is Zhang Bao; his mother was née Hou, and his stepmothers are née Yang and née Sun. Both parents are living. His younger brothers are Mu, Xiao, Jiao, Zi, Gong, and Yiming. He married née Xu. He placed sixty-fifth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕惟自古
帝王撫運握圖統
一寰宇所以綜輯
庶務調劑羣品其
道盖多端矣至語
===
其治效自詩書所
述章灼較著則莫
盛於虞周夫其七
政齊庶尹諧六府
修三事治與夫謨
alt_text:
皇帝制曰朕惟自古
帝王撫運握圖統

庶務調劑羣品其
道葢多端矣至語
===
其治效自詩書所
述章灼較著則莫
盛於虞周夫其七
政齊庶尹諧六府
修三事治與夫謨
punctuated: 皇帝制曰：朕惟自古帝王撫運握圖，統一寰宇，所以綜輯庶務、調劑羣品，其道盖多端矣。至語其治效，自《詩》、《書》所述，章灼較著，則莫盛於虞、周。夫其七政齊，庶尹諧，六府修，三事治，與夫謨
translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: We reflect that since antiquity, emperors and kings who have embraced the Mandate, held the royal chart, and unified the realm have employed manifold ways to bring together the myriad affairs of state and harmonize the multitude of beings. Yet when speaking of the efficacy of their governance, among what is recounted in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu) as brilliantly manifest and clearly evident, none was more flourishing than in the eras of Yu [Shun] and Zhou. Now, as for how the seven celestial governors were aligned, the various officials were in harmony, the six treasuries of nature were well-maintained, and the three affairs were well-governed, along with how the counsels…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
烈佑啓禮樂刑政
煥然也朕甚嘉之
慕之未審果繇何
道而致然歟或謂
舜兢業萬幾文王
===
自朝至日中昃不
遑食也唯其精勤
故化理若是然書
稱庶獄庶慎文王
罔兼而孔子復謂
alt_text:
烈佑啓禮樂刑政
煥然也朕甚嘉之
慕之未審果繇何
道而致然歟或謂
舜堯業萬幾文王
===
自朝至日中昃不
遑食也唯其精勤
故化理若是然書
稱庶獄庶慎文王
罔兼而孔子復謂
punctuated: 烈佑啓，禮樂刑政煥然也。朕甚嘉之、慕之，未審果繇何道而致然歟？或謂舜兢業萬幾，文王自朝至日中昃不遑食也；唯其精勤，故化理若是。然《書》稱庶獄庶慎，文王罔兼，而孔子復謂
translation_en: …resplendent plans that aided and enlightened posterity, and how rituals, music, punishments, and governance shone forth so brilliantly. We deeply admire and yearn for this, yet We have not discerned by what Way such governance was truly brought about. Some say that Shun attended to the myriad affairs with cautious diligence, and that King Wen from morning until noon and the declining sun had no leisure to eat; only because of their focused diligence did their transformative ordering reach such a state. Yet the Book of Documents (Shu) states that with regard to the numerous judicial cases and the numerous cautionary matters, King Wen did not personally combine them all in his own hands; and Confucius furthermore said that…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
舜無爲而治何歟
我
太祖神聖乗乾再造
函夏建立法制博
大詳密用以躋世
===
平康與虞周媲盛
矣御曆三十餘年
早朝晏罷未嘗時
刻少怠其所以畏
天人而衍昌祚者
alt_text:
舜無爲而治何歟
我
太祖神聖秉乾再造
函夏建立法制博
大詳密用以躋世
平康與虞周媲盛
矣御曆三十餘年
早朝晏罷未嘗時
刻少怠其所以畏
天人而行昌祚者
punctuated: 舜「無爲而治」，何歟？我太祖神聖乗乾，再造函夏，建立法制，博大詳密，用以躋世平康，與虞、周媲盛矣。御曆三十餘年，早朝晏罷，未嘗時刻少怠。其所以畏天人而衍昌祚者，
translation_en: … that Shun “governed by non-action”—why is this? Our Grand Progenitor (Taizu 太祖), divinely sage, ascended the throne and remade the Chinese realm. He established laws and institutions that were broad, grand, detailed, and thorough, thereby raising the world to peace and prosperity, rivaling the flourishing eras of Yu [Shun] and Zhou. Holding the calendar of reign for more than thirty years, he held court early in the morning and retired late in the evening, never relaxing even for a moment. The way in which he stood in awe of Heaven and man and extended our prosperous imperial line—…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
視舜文其道同歟
朕以冲昧獲纘丕
基慄慄夙夜圖所
以順帝則建皇極
以庶幾帝王之治
===
者今且五年經費
節矣而帑庾未充
賦歛寬矣而民生
寡遂守宰乆任矣
而吏治罔宣伍籍
alt_text:
視舜文其道同歟
朕以沖昧獲纘丕
基慄慄夙夜圖所
以順帝則建皇極
以庶幾帝王之治
===
者今且五年經費
節矣而帑庾未充
賦歛寛矣而民生
寡遂守宰久任矣
而吏治罔宣伍籍
punctuated: 視舜、文，其道同歟？朕以冲昧，獲纘丕基，慄慄夙夜，圖所以順帝則、建皇極，以庶幾帝王之治者，今且五年。經費節矣，而帑庾未充；賦歛寬矣，而民生寡遂；守宰乆任矣，而吏治罔宣；伍籍
translation_en:
…Compared with Shun and King Wen, was his Way the same?

In my youth and inexperience, I have succeeded to the great foundation. Trembling with awe day and night, I have sought to follow the Heavenly principles and establish the August Ultimate, hoping to approximate the governance of the ancient emperors and kings, for what is now nearly five years. Regular expenditures have been curtailed, yet the treasuries and granaries are still not full; taxes and levies have been relaxed, yet the people's livelihoods are rarely secure; prefects and magistrates have been kept long in office, yet administrative governance is not made manifest; the military registers…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
加覈矣而武備靡
振豈因循之積習
難驟變歟久弛之
舊章難遽舉歟茲
欲革文冒破拘攣
===
使人得其情事循
其理將何如而後
可盖盛帝顯王人
稱之必曰大有爲
乃復有謂王者中
alt_text:
加覈矣而武備廢
振豈因循之積習
難驟變歟久弛之
舊章難遽舉歟茲
欲革文冒破拘攣
===
使人得其情事循
其理將何如而後
可盖盛帝顯王人
稱之必曰大有爲
乃復有謂王者中
punctuated: 加覈矣，而武備靡振。豈因循之積習難驟變歟？久弛之舊章難遽舉歟？茲欲革文冒，破拘攣，使人得其情，事循其理，將何如而後可？盖盛帝顯王，人稱之必曰「大有爲」，乃復有謂「王者中心無為，以守至正」…
translation_en: …have been further verified, yet military preparedness has not been revitalized. Is it that deeply entrenched habits of routine and complacency are difficult to change suddenly, or that long-relaxed old regulations are difficult to reinstate abruptly? Now, if We wish to eliminate formalistic pretension and fraud, break away from rigid constraints, enable people to realize their genuine capabilities, and ensure that affairs follow their proper principles, how are We to proceed so that this may be achieved? Indeed, when people praise flourishing emperors and illustrious kings, they invariably speak of them as "achieving great things," yet there is also the saying that "a true king holds to non-action in his heart so as to guard the utmost rectitude"…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
心無為以守至正
此其說安是將各
有主謂不相蒙歟
抑或其道相須也
子大夫習先聖之
===
術其於古今治理
之原講之豫矣尚
各攄所蘊明著于
篇朕將覽而擇焉
alt_text:
心無爲以守至正
此其說安是將各
有主謂不相蒙歟
抑或其道相須也
子大夫習先聖之
===
術其於古今治理
之原講之豫矣尚
各攄所藴明著于
篇朕將覽而擇焉
punctuated: 心無為，以守至正。此其說安是？將各有主謂，不相蒙歟？抑或其道相須也？子大夫習先聖之術，其於古今治理之原，講之豫矣。尚各攄所蘊，明著于篇，朕將覽而擇焉。
translation_en: … remains inactive in his heart so as to preserve the utmost rectitude. Which of these doctrines is right? Does each have its own focus so that they have no bearing on each other, or do their principles complement one another? You gentlemen have studied the arts of the former sages, and regarding the origins of governance in ancient and modern times, you have examined them thoroughly beforehand. May each of you set forth what you have stored up within and state it clearly in your essays; We shall peruse them and make Our selection therefrom.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
臣沈懋學
臣對臣聞帝王之御世也固有宰制天下之
大體尤有運量天下之大機何謂體總宏綱
急先務任人以圖治而不自用以勞天下者
是也何謂機凝志慮勵臣工及時以省成而
不自逸以忘天下者是也以大體宰制天下
則化洽於無為而帝則順矣以大機運量天
下則功成於有為而皇極建矣是其無為也
正以操有為之權也而非逸也其有為也正
以達無為之用也而非勞也使執有為之說
===
而紛然自勞其身則萬幾之繁萬民之衆由
一人而叢挫焉即或有刑名之淺效而無以
培惇大之休申韓之所謂有為也固非帝王
之所先使泥無為之說而肆然自逸其身則
萬幾之繁萬民之衆以一人而廢弛焉即或
有清淨之小康而無以建精明之治黃老之
所謂無為也亦豈帝王之所尚哉是故善治
天下者既不一於有為而機常運於無為之
中又不一於無為而體常宰於有為之際古
帝王所以人得其情事循其理而萬世稱之

punctuated:
臣沈懋學。
臣對：臣聞帝王之御世也，固有宰制天下之大體，尤有運量天下之大機。何謂體？總宏綱、急先務，任人以圖治而不自用以勞天下者是也。何謂機？凝志慮、勵臣工，及時以省成而不自逸以忘天下者是也。以大體宰制天下，則化洽於無為，而帝則順矣；以大機運量天下，則功成於有為，而皇極建矣。是其無為也，正以操有為之權也，而非逸也；其有為也，正以達無為之用也，而非勞也。使執有為之說，而紛然自勞其身，則萬幾之繁、萬民之衆，由一人而叢挫焉，即或有刑名之淺效，而無以培惇大之休，申、韓之所謂有為也，固非帝王之所先；使泥無為之說，而肆然自逸其身，則萬幾之繁、萬民之衆，以一人而廢弛焉，即或有清淨之小康，而無以建精明之治，黃、老之所謂無為也，亦豈帝王之所尚哉！是故善治天下者，既不一於有為，而機常運於無為之中；又不一於無為，而體常宰於有為之際。古帝王所以人得其情、事循其理，而萬世稱之
translation_en:
Your servant Shen Maoxue 沈懋學.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when emperors and kings govern the world, they certainly possess the great fundamental principle for presiding over and regulating the realm, and even more so possess the great dynamic mechanism for directing and measuring out the realm. What is meant by the fundamental principle? It is grasping the grand outline and prioritizing urgent tasks, entrusting others to plan for good governance rather than relying solely on oneself and thereby exhausting the realm. What is meant by the dynamic mechanism? It is focusing one's will and deliberations and encouraging the officials, examining accomplishments in a timely manner rather than indulging in personal ease and thereby forgetting the realm. When one presides over and regulates the realm through the great fundamental principle, moral transformation pervades through non-action (wuwei), and the imperial pattern is顺 [harmoniously followed]; when one directs and measures out the realm through the great dynamic mechanism, achievements are brought to completion through purposeful action (youwei), and the August Ultimate is established. Thus, his non-action is precisely the means by which he holds the authority of purposeful action, and is not mere ease; his purposeful action is precisely the means by which he fulfills the function of non-action, and is not mere toil. 

Suppose one were to cling to the doctrine of purposeful action and busily wear out one's own person; then the myriad affairs in their complexity and the myriad people in their multitude would become bogged down and frustrated in petty details on account of a single man. Even if there might be some shallow results from the methods of punishments and names (xingming), there would be no way to cultivate the blessings of generous magnanimity. This is what Shen Buhai 申不害 and Han Fei 韓非 called purposeful action, and it is certainly not what emperors and kings put first. Suppose one were to be bogged down in the doctrine of non-action and unrestrainedly indulge one's own person in ease; then the myriad affairs in their complexity and the myriad people in their multitude would fall into neglect and laxity on account of a single man. Even if there might be a minor tranquility of pure quietude, there would be no way to establish a vigorous and clear-sighted governance. This is what the Yellow Emperor 黃帝 and Laozi 老子 called non-action, and how could it be what emperors and kings esteem! 

Therefore, one who is skilled at governing the realm neither commits exclusively to purposeful action—for the dynamic mechanism constantly operates within non-action—nor commits exclusively to non-action—for the fundamental principle constantly presides amid purposeful action. The reason the ancient emperors and kings enabled people to fulfill their true dispositions and affairs to follow their proper principles, so that ten thousand generations praised them…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
為盛德大業者此道行也歟欽惟
皇帝陛下
稟聰明睿智之資
備文武聖神之德應五百載之昌期而誕膺
寶曆繼億萬年之正統而不振
瑤圖
威德布於華夷賢才列於中外四時順軌萬國承
休人已安事已治矣而猶
聖不自聖進臣等於
廷俯賜
===
清問惓惓於有為無為之辨且欲使人得其情事
循其理以圖帝王之治臣固仰窺
陛下大有為之心矣顧臣伏處蓬藋未知事君之
道未諳治國之謨愧無以對揚萬一雖然臣
嘗聞之事君如事親親之欲有為也子代之
親之精神日運於上下內外之間而庶事則
未嘗自勞也知所以事親而孝可移於忠矣
又聞之治國如治家家之不能無為也主制
之應酬出納至米鹽瑣屑之務各有司存而
主之精神未嘗不貫也知所以治家而理可

廷俯賜
===

親之精神日運於上下內外之間而庶事則
未甞自勞也知所以事親而孝可移於忠矣

之應酬出納至米鹽瑣屑之務各有司存而
主之精神未甞不貫也知所以治家而理可
punctuated:
為盛德大業者，此道行也歟！

欽惟皇帝陛下，稟聰明睿智之資，備文武聖神之德，應五百載之昌期而誕膺寶曆，繼億萬年之正統而不振瑤圖。威德布於華夷，賢才列於中外，四時順軌，萬國承休，人已安、事已治矣。而猶聖不自聖，進臣等於廷，俯賜清問，惓惓於有為無為之辨，且欲使人得其情、事循其理，以圖帝王之治。臣固仰窺陛下大有為之心矣。顧臣伏處蓬藋，未知事君之道，未諳治國之謨，愧無以對揚萬一。雖然，臣嘗聞之：事君如事親。親之欲有為也，子代之；親之精神日運於上下內外之間，而庶事則未嘗自勞也。知所以事親，而孝可移於忠矣。又聞之：治國如治家。家之不能無為也，主制之；應酬出納，至米鹽瑣屑之務，各有司存，而主之精神未嘗不貫也。知所以治家，而理可
translation_en:
… as flourishing virtue and great enterprise—was it not because this Way was practiced?

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed with a nature of keen perception and profound wisdom, and possesses the virtues of civil and martial accomplishment, sageliness, and spiritual insight. Answering the prosperous epoch that comes once in five hundred years, You have grandly received the precious calendar; succeeding to the legitimate line of ten thousand myriad years, You greatly[?] rouse the jade-like realm. Your majesty and virtue are spread among Chinese and non-Chinese alike; worthy talents are arrayed at court and in the provinces; the four seasons follow their regular courses; the myriad states receive Your blessings; the people are already at peace and affairs are already well-governed. Yet even in Your sageliness You do not regard Yourself as sage, advancing Your servants and others to the court and graciously bestowing Your pure inquiry. You are earnestly concerned with the distinction between active exertion and non-action, and furthermore wish to ensure that people attain their proper dispositions and affairs follow their proper principles, so as to plan for the governance of the ancient emperors and kings. Your servant indeed looks up and catches a glimpse of Your Majesty's mind bent on great accomplishments.

Yet Your servant has lived in obscurity among weeds and brambles, not yet knowing the way of serving a ruler and unfamiliar with the counsels for governing a state, and is ashamed to have nothing with which to respond to and extol even one ten-thousandth of Your inquiry. Even so, Your servant has heard it said: serving a ruler is like serving one's parents. When parents wish to accomplish something, the son does it on their behalf; the parents' spirit and attention circulate daily between above and below, inside and outside, while they never toil personally over routine matters. When one knows how to serve one's parents, filial piety can be transferred into loyalty. I have also heard it said: governing a state is like managing a household. Where a household cannot do without active management, the master directs it; as for social intercourse, receipts and expenditures, down to the trivial matters of rice and salt, each has its own person in charge, yet the master's spirit and attention never fail to penetrate them all. When one knows how to manage a household, its principles can…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
通於國矣况臣今藉有司之舉得親
文陛立
赤墀生平之所誦讀願達於天下見於
明時者此可以酬其志也敢不攄一得之愚備
聖人之擇哉竊惟天生民而不能以自治也於是
立之君以主之又慮君不能以獨治也於是
立之臣以佐之是君者代天以理物而臣者
代君以有終者也君惟代天以理物則天之
所欲為者君任之矣而安可以無為也臣惟
代君以有終則君之所欲為者臣任之矣而
===
無庸於自為也甞觀之天矣於穆之真玄機
之宰凝然不動已耳而四時之吏五行之佐
順序而成其化化之成也四時五行之功而
昊天一元之運固未甞一日息也使其或息
則四時五行且無以自運而何有於化哉夫
自其凝然不動而四時五行為之宣其化也
謂天有為不可也是天之體也自其四時五
行之成化而天未甞不運也謂天無為不可
也是天之機也人君代天而為之子位曰天
位職曰天職民曰天民德曰天德道曰天道

通於國矣。况臣今藉有司之舉，得親文陛，立赤墀，生平之所誦讀，願達於天下、見於明時者，此可以酬其志也，敢不攄一得之愚，備聖人之擇哉？

竊惟天生民而不能以自治也，於是立之君以主之；又慮君不能以獨治也，於是立之臣以佐之。是君者，代天以理物；而臣者，代君以有終者也。君惟代天以理物，則天之所欲為者，君任之矣，而安可以無為也？臣惟代君以有終，則君之所欲為者，臣任之矣，而無庸於自為也。

甞觀之天矣，於穆之真，玄機之宰，凝然不動已耳，而四時之吏、五行之佐，順序而成其化。化之成也，四時、五行之功，而昊天一元之運，固未甞一日息也。使其或息，則四時、五行且無以自運，而何有於化哉？夫自其凝然不動，而四時、五行為之宣其化也，謂天有為，不可也，是天之體也；自其四時、五行之成化，而天未甞不運也，謂天無為，不可也，是天之機也。人君代天而為之子，位曰天位，職曰天職，民曰天民，德曰天德，道曰天道，
translation_en:
… be extended to the state. How much more so now that your servant, relying on the recommendation of the authorities, has been able to approach the cultured steps of the throne and stand upon the crimson courtyard! What I have recited and studied all my life, hoping to extend throughout the Empire and manifest in this enlightened age, can hereby fulfill my aspirations. How dare I not pour forth my humble, single-minded understanding to offer it for the Sage's selection?

I humbly reflect that Heaven gives birth to the people, yet they cannot govern themselves; therefore, it establishes a ruler to preside over them. Furthermore, concerned that the ruler cannot govern alone, it establishes ministers to assist him. Thus, the ruler acts on behalf of Heaven to order all things, while the ministers act on behalf of the ruler to bring matters to completion. Because the ruler acts on behalf of Heaven to order all things, what Heaven wishes to do becomes the responsibility of the ruler—how then could he take no action? Because the ministers act on behalf of the ruler to bring matters to completion, what the ruler wishes to do becomes the responsibility of the ministers—and thus the ruler has no need to do everything himself.

I have observed this in Heaven: in its profound and solemn reality, the master of the mysterious mechanism simply remains poised and unmoving, while the officials of the four seasons and the assistants of the Five Phases follow their proper sequence to accomplish its transformations. The completion of transformation is the achievement of the four seasons and the Five Phases, yet the revolution of vast Heaven's primordial vitality has never ceased for a single day. Were it ever to cease, the four seasons and the Five Phases would have no means to revolve on their own, and what transformation could there be? Viewed from the perspective that it remains poised and unmoving while the four seasons and Five Phases proclaim its transformations on its behalf, one cannot say that Heaven takes action; this is the substance of Heaven. Viewed from the perspective that the four seasons and Five Phases accomplish transformation while Heaven never ceases to revolve, one cannot say that Heaven takes no action; this is the vital mechanism of Heaven. The human ruler acts on behalf of Heaven as its Son: his position is called the Heavenly position, his office is called the Heavenly office, his people are called the Heavenly people, his virtue is called the Heavenly virtue, his Way is called the Heavenly Way, …

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
心曰天心而不憲天以弘化可乎是故觀於
之體也得宰制天下之大體焉虛心應物
而不以物累心虛己任人而不以人役己常
處於閒靜之中以總宏綱以急先務固不敢
屑屑焉以自勞觀於天之機也得運量天下
之大機焉心常運物而不縱心以遺物己常
體人而不適己以病人獨操夫精勤之柄以
凝志慮以勵臣工亦不敢悠悠焉以自逸惟
其有是體也人代之爲矣安得而不謂之無
爲惟其有是機也己爲之運矣安得而不謂
===
之有爲而要之有爲者乃所以成其無爲也
百工之熙必率作而後興事惇大之裕必明
作而後有功萬世帝王撫運握圖統一寰宇
所以綜輯庶務調劑羣生者其道寧外於此
乎是故七政齊庶尹諧六府修三事治治效
莫盛於虞矣舜固不自爲也任之禹益羲和
臯夔諸臣者得其體也而兢業萬幾舜寔未
嘗一日而忘精勤之慮焉然則孔子稱其無
爲而治者謂其所任得人耳豈曰兢業可忘
耶謨烈啓後咸正罔缺禮樂刑政煥然維新

punctuated: 心曰天心，而不憲天以弘化，可乎？是故觀於之體也，得宰制天下之大體焉：虛心應物而不以物累心，虛己任人而不以人役己，常處於閒靜之中，以總宏綱、以急先務，固不敢屑屑焉以自勞。觀於天之機也，得運量天下之大機焉：心常運物而不縱心以遺物，己常體人而不適己以病人，獨操夫精勤之柄，以凝志慮、以勵臣工，亦不敢悠悠焉以自逸。惟其有是體也，人代之爲矣，安得而不謂之無爲？惟其有是機也，己爲之運矣，安得而不謂之有爲？而要之，有爲者乃所以成其無爲也。百工之熙，必率作而後興事；惇大之裕，必明作而後有功。萬世帝王撫運握圖、統一寰宇，所以綜輯庶務、調劑羣生者，其道寧外於此乎？是故七政齊，庶尹諧，六府修，三事治，治效莫盛於虞矣。舜固不自爲也，任之禹、益、羲、和、臯、夔諸臣者，得其體也；而兢業萬幾，舜寔未嘗一日而忘精勤之慮焉。然則孔子稱其「無爲而治」者，謂其所任得人耳，豈曰兢業可忘耶？謨烈啓後，咸正罔缺，禮樂刑政，煥然維新，
translation_en: …his mind is called Heaven's mind—could he fail to model himself upon Heaven in order to broaden transformation? Therefore, by observing [Heaven's] substance, he grasps the great substance of governing the realm: with an empty mind he responds to things without letting things burden his mind; with an empty self he delegates to others without letting himself be enslaved on account of others; he abides constantly in serene tranquility in order to hold together the grand guidelines and attend urgently to primary duties, certainly never daring to weary himself over petty details. By observing the mechanism of Heaven, he grasps the great mechanism for revolving and measuring the realm: his mind constantly directs things without indulging itself so as to neglect them; he himself is constantly considerate of others without gratifying himself to the detriment of others; he alone wields the handle of assiduous diligence in order to focus his intentions and thoughts and to spur on his officials, likewise never daring to lapse into idle ease. Because he possesses this substance, others act on his behalf—how could this not be called non-action (wuwei)? Because he possesses this mechanism, he himself sets it in motion—how could this not be called action (youwei)? Yet in sum, action is precisely the means by which non-action is achieved. For the accomplishments of the hundred officials to flourish, one must lead them in action before enterprises can rise; for the abundance of generous magnanimity to be realized, one must act with clear vigor before merit can be achieved. As monarchs across ten thousand generations respond to destiny, hold the imperial chart, and unify the world, how could the Way by which they synthesize the myriad affairs and harmonize all living beings lie outside of this? Therefore, when the Seven Directors were aligned, the hundred officials were in harmony, the Six Treasuries were in order, and the Three Affairs were governed, the efficacy of rule was never more flourishing than under Yu [Shun]. Shun certainly did not do everything himself; by entrusting affairs to such ministers as Yu, Yi, Xi, He, Gao [Yao], and Kui, he attained the proper substance. Yet in being cautious and fearful over the myriad affairs of state, Shun truly never for a single day forgot his thoughts of assiduous diligence. Thus, when Confucius praised him for "governing by non-action," he meant only that Shun had found the right men to entrust—how could he have meant that caution and diligence may be forgotten? When grand plans and meritorious deeds opened the way for posterity, when all was rectified without defect, and when rites, music, punishments, and administration were brilliantly renewed,…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
治效莫盛乎周矣文固不自爲也任之周召
呂散諸臣者得其體也而自朝至於日昃不
遑食文寔未甞一日而忘精勤之慮焉然則
書稱庶慎庶獄罔兼者正謂其所任得人耳
豈曰勵精可已耶洪惟我
太祖高皇帝神聖乗乾再造函夏竭心思以創制
立法內外相維巨細畢舉具載
令甲今不暇殫述而御曆三十餘年早朝晏罷
未甞時刻少怠其所以畏天人而衍昌祚者
真如舜之兢業萬幾文之日昃不食固未甞
===
執無爲之說忘率作之權而君臣交儆以屢
省厥成者正所以成無爲之化也躋世平康
虞周媲盛信有由矣而誰謂其道之不同於
舜文哉肆我
皇上講學勤政法天行而不息詢事考言治日超
而有功帝王之大經大法治天下之宏規也
大書而揭諸
殿廷自敬天至節用十二事治天下之切務也
懸牌而置之
座右申飭有司而責之久任屢警邊將而要其

punctuated: 治效莫盛乎周矣。文固不自爲也，任之周、召、呂、散諸臣者，得其體也；而自朝至於日昃，不遑食，文寔未甞一日而忘精勤之慮焉。然則《書》稱「庶慎、庶獄罔兼」者，正謂其所任得人耳，豈曰勵精可已耶？洪惟我太祖高皇帝，神聖乗乾，再造函夏，竭心思以創制立法，內外相維，巨細畢舉，具載令甲，今不暇殫述；而御曆三十餘年，早朝晏罷，未甞時刻少怠。其所以畏天人而衍昌祚者，真如舜之兢業萬幾、文之日昃不食，固未甞執無爲之說、忘率作之權，而君臣交儆以屢省厥成者，正所以成無爲之化也。躋世平康，虞、周媲盛，信有由矣，而誰謂其道之不同於舜、文哉？肆我皇上，講學勤政，法天行而不息；詢事考言，治日超而有功。帝王之大經大法，治天下之宏規也，大書而揭諸殿廷；自敬天至節用十二事，治天下之切務也，懸牌而置之座右。申飭有司而責之久任，屢警邊將而要其
translation_en:
…and no achievements of governance were more flourishing than those of the Zhou! King Wen certainly did not do everything himself; in delegating to such ministers as the Duke of Zhou, the Duke of Shao, Lü Shang, and San Yisheng, he grasped the essential body of rule. Yet from morning until the sun slanted westward he had no leisure to eat; in truth, King Wen never for a single day forgot his thoughts of diligent exertion. Why, then, does the Book of Documents praise him for "not personally doubling in the various precautions and various judicial cases"? It simply means that he obtained the right men to entrust with office—how could it mean that vigorous diligence might be abandoned?

I humbly reflect upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu): divinely sage, he mounted the throne and recreated the Chinese realm. He exhausted his mind and thoughts in establishing institutions and enacting laws, whereby the inner and outer domains mutually sustained one another and matters great and small were all set in motion. These are fully recorded in the imperial statutes, and I have not the leisure to recount them all here. Yet throughout his reign of more than thirty years, he held court early and retired late, never slackening for a single moment. The way in which he stood in awe of Heaven and man and prolonged our prosperous destiny was truly like Shun's cautious diligence in the myriad affairs of state and King Wen's having no leisure to eat until sunset. He certainly never clung to the doctrine of non-action so as to forget his authority to lead and initiate; rather, sovereign and ministers mutually admonishing one another and repeatedly examining their accomplishments was precisely the means by which the transformative influence of non-action was achieved. That he raised the world to peace and tranquility, matching the splendor of Yu and Zhou, truly had its cause! And who would say that his Way differed from that of Shun and King Wen?

Thus our Emperor pursues learning and is diligent in governance, modeling himself on the ceaseless movement of Heaven; he inquiries into affairs and examines words, so that governance daily advances and achieves results. The great norms and great laws of emperors and kings are the grand plans for governing the empire, and he has had them written in large script and displayed in the palace halls; the twelve matters, from revering Heaven to economizing on expenditures, are the urgent tasks of governing the empire, and he has had them inscribed on plaques placed to the right of his throne. He repeatedly admonishes the authorities and holds them to long tenures of office; he frequently warns the frontier generals and demands that they secure…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
久安蠲逋賦以厚民生節經費以裕國計孜
孜焉精勤之念誠有不遑暇豫者宜天下之
人盡得其情事盡循其理也而乃有不然者
宜有以厪
聖心之憂矣夫因循之積習固難驟更也而更之
者未必有實心久弛之舊章固難遽舉也而
舉之者未必有實政欲充帑庾而司農之用
果實能一毫不妄費乎節儉之躬行不可不
思也欲厚民生而司賦之吏果實能一毫不
妄取乎閭閻之疾苦不可不察也守令久任
===
===
矣而率多取辦於文具求其能解紛興化鮮
渤海之理也而何惑乎吏治之未宣伍籍加
覈矣而率多致飾於聲容求其能禦侮折衝
鮮鴈門之良也而何惑乎武備之靡振夫臣
未盡賢而政未盡實則
陛下與諸大臣議政於上恐未可遽云舜之無為
文之無憂也夫古今之人心一也以區區漢
宣之綜核即能回虛耗之邦致吏稱民安之
效曾謂
今日寧平之世乃令之而不從倡之而不化耶

今日寧平之世乃令之而不從倡之而不化耶
punctuated: 久安，蠲逋賦以厚民生，節經費以裕國計，孜孜焉精勤之念，誠有不遑暇豫者。宜天下之人盡得其情，事盡循其理也；而乃有不然者，宜有以厪聖心之憂矣。夫因循之積習，固難驟更也，而更之者未必有實心；久弛之舊章，固難遽舉也，而舉之者未必有實政。欲充帑庾，而司農之用果實能一毫不妄費乎？節儉之躬行，不可不思也。欲厚民生，而司賦之吏果實能一毫不妄取乎？閭閻之疾苦，不可不察也。守令久任矣，而率多取辦於文具，求其能解紛興化，鮮渤海之理也，而何惑乎吏治之未宣？伍籍加覈矣，而率多致飾於聲容，求其能禦侮折衝，鮮鴈門之良也，而何惑乎武備之靡振？夫臣未盡賢，而政未盡實，則陛下與諸大臣議政於上，恐未可遽云舜之無為、文之無憂也。夫古今之人心一也，以區區漢宣之綜核，即能回虛耗之邦，致吏稱民安之效，曾謂今日寧平之世，乃令之而不從，倡之而不化耶？
translation_en:
…lasting peace; remitting tax arrears so as to enrich the people's livelihood; and curtailing regular expenditures so as to make the state finances abundant. Tirelessly and with devoted diligence, You truly leave Yourself no time for leisure or comfort. It ought to be that all people in the realm have their circumstances understood and all affairs follow their proper principles. Yet there are respects in which this is not so, which rightly causes anxiety in Your Sacred Mind.

Now, entrenched habits of perfunctory routine are assuredly hard to alter all at once, and those who would alter them do not necessarily possess a sincere heart; long-relaxed old statutes are assuredly hard to revive suddenly, and those who would revive them do not necessarily carry out substantive governance. We wish to fill the treasuries and granaries, yet in the expenditures of the Ministry of Revenue (Sinong), are they truly able not to waste a single shred? The personal practice of frugality cannot but be pondered. We wish to enrich the people's livelihood, yet among the tax-collecting officials, are they truly able not to extort a single shred? The sufferings of the common folk in their villages cannot but be investigated.

Prefects and Magistrates (Shouling) have been kept long in office, yet for the most part they merely get by through outward formalities; if one seeks those capable of resolving disorders and promoting moral transformation, few match the governance of Bohai [by Gong Sui under the Han]—so what wonder is it that administrative governance has not been diffused? The military registers have been subjected to closer verification, yet for the most part they merely dress up appearances and pomp; if one seeks those capable of repelling aggression and breaking enemy assaults, few match the excellence of Yanmen [under Li Mu]—so what wonder is it that military preparedness has not been invigorated?

When ministers are not all worthy and governance is not all substantive, then even as Your Majesty deliberates on state affairs above with the various Grand Ministers, I fear one cannot yet readily speak of Shun's non-action or King Wen's freedom from worry. Yet the human heart is the same in ancient and modern times. Even with the mere comprehensive verification of Emperor Xuan of the Han, he was able to restore a depleted and exhausted state and achieve the result of officials being equal to their duties and the people being at peace. Could it be said that in today's age of peace and tranquility, people are commanded yet do not obey, or led yet are not transformed?

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
陛下誠率先而振作之不厭乎感格之難不循乎
故常之迹時
召見二三大臣及百司之可與議者條
國家之舊典舉當世之闕遺必欲見之推行而
要之治效實節經費自
宮闈先之而帑庾可漸充矣實寛斂賦自郊圻
先之而民生可漸厚矣任守令則
嚴敕監司精愼舉劾毋徒徇于文具而吏治可漸
宣矣覈伍籍則
嚴敕督撫糾察勤惰毋觀美于聲容而武備可漸
===
振矣其要主於擇人而其權歸於核實由是
文冒可革拘攣可破積習可更舊章可舉人
不敢欺而皆得其情事不敢廢而皆循其理
而本其機則惟在
陛下與二三大臣如舜文之精勤以率之夫然後
庶愼庶獄不必兼而無爲之化成矣夫此之
所謂精勤云者有爲之義也而因以致無爲
焉猶二之也臣又伏讀
聖制終篇有曰盛帝顯王人稱之必曰大有爲乃
復有謂王者中心無爲以守至正此其說安是

punctuated:
陛下誠率先而振作之，不厭乎感格之難，不循乎故常之迹，時召見二三大臣及百司之可與議者，條國家之舊典，舉當世之闕遺，必欲見之推行，而要之治效。實節經費，自宮闈先之，而帑庾可漸充矣；實寛斂賦，自郊圻先之，而民生可漸厚矣；任守令，則嚴敕監司精愼舉劾，毋徒徇于文具，而吏治可漸宣矣；覈伍籍，則嚴敕督撫糾察勤惰，毋觀美于聲容，而武備可漸振矣。其要主於擇人，而其權歸於核實。由是，文冒可革，拘攣可破，積習可更，舊章可舉，人不敢欺而皆得其情，事不敢廢而皆循其理。而本其機，則惟在陛下與二三大臣如舜、文之精勤以率之。夫然後庶愼庶獄不必兼，而無爲之化成矣。

夫此之所謂精勤云者，有爲之義也，而因以致無爲焉，猶二之也。臣又伏讀聖制，終篇有曰：「盛帝顯王，人稱之必曰大有爲，乃復有謂王者中心無爲以守至正。此其說安是？
translation_en:
If Your Majesty truly takes the lead in rousing action, neither tiring of the difficulty of moving people's hearts nor merely following the ruts of old routine, and frequently summons the two or three Grand Ministers along with those among the hundred officials who are worthy of consultation to itemize the old statutes of the Dynasty and point out the omissions and shortcomings of the present age, insisting on seeing them carried into practice and demanding actual results in governance: then by genuinely curtailing expenditures—beginning first within the palace precincts—the treasuries and granaries can gradually be replenished; by genuinely relaxing the collection of taxes—beginning first in the suburban domains—the people's livelihood can gradually be enriched; in employing Prefects and Magistrates, by strictly instructing the Surveillance Officials to be scrupulous and cautious in recommendations and impeachments rather than merely complying with empty formalities, official administration can gradually be diffused; in verifying the military registers, by strictly instructing the Supreme Commanders and Grand Coordinators to investigate diligence and negligence rather than admiring superficial displays of sound and appearance, military preparedness can gradually be revitalized. The essential point lies in selecting the right men, and the authority rests in verifying realities. Thereby, fraudulent pretenses can be eliminated, rigid constraints can be broken, accumulated habits can be changed, and old regulations can be restored; men will not dare to deceive and the true circumstances of all will be ascertained, while affairs will not dare to be neglected and all will follow their proper principles. Tracing the pivotal mechanism to its root, it rests solely upon Your Majesty and the two or three Grand Ministers leading the way with the focused diligence of Shun and King Wen. Only then will it be unnecessary to personally attend to all the myriad precautions and myriad lawsuits, and the transformative influence of non-action (wuwei) will be accomplished.

Now, what is here called focused diligence has the meaning of purposeful action (youwei), yet using it as a means to attain non-action still treats the two as separate. Your servant has also humbly read Your Majesty's Sacred Decree, which at the close of the text says: "When people speak of flourishing emperors and illustrious kings, they invariably call them rulers of great purposeful action; yet there is also the saying that the true king maintains non-action in the center of his heart so as to guard supreme rectitude. Which of these doctrines is right? …

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
將各有主謂不相蒙歟抑或其道相須也噫是
可以觀帝王經綸之學矣夫中心無爲矣而
曰以守至正得非守之於爲乎昊天之道顯
仁藏用曰顯曰藏而有爲無爲體用一原矣
帝王之大有爲也以天運以時行而不以己
爲焉則雖淵微宥密而非無也雖振勵發舒
而非有也故曰至誠經綸而無所倚也彼沉
空守寂以爲無徇生執象以爲有均之畔道
而已惡足以治天下噫天下之溺久矣談有
爲者猶曰不離乎倫物也而假禪幻之苴餘
===
以文其無爲之旨卒使天下信空虛而忘實
用而精勤之說幾不復聞矣
陛下循其名必責其實虞其始必厚其終以至誠
之經綸發顯藏之妙用不將挽人心而維世
道乎而得情循理之效又不足言矣此眞大
有爲之略也若夫爲知幾爲謹獨固至誠入
德之方而自警十二事所兼括也何敢爲費
辭哉臣不識忌諱干冒
宸嚴不勝戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

translation_en:
… Does each have its own focus so that they have nothing to do with one another, or do their principles mutually depend on each other?"

Ah! In this one may observe the learning of emperors and kings in ordering the realm. Now, when the heart within engages in non-action, yet it is said "thereby preserving the utmost correctness," is this not preserving it through action? The Way of August Heaven manifests benevolence and conceals its function; in speaking of manifestation and concealment, active striving and non-action share a single source of substance and function. In the great active striving of emperors and kings, they move with Heaven and act according to the times, without acting out of personal will. Thus, though deep, subtle, and serenely quiet, it is not nothingness; though vigorous, roused, and expansive, it is not contrived action. Therefore it is said that utmost sincerity orders the realm without leaning on anything. Those who sink into emptiness and guard quiescence, taking that as non-action, or who chase after life and cling to outward forms, taking that as action, alike merely rebel against the Way—how could they suffice to govern the world?

Ah! The world has been drowning for a long time. Those who speak of active striving still say that it does not depart from human relationships and affairs; yet those who borrow the dregs of Chan Buddhist illusions to embellish their doctrine of non-action end up causing the world to believe in emptiness and forget practical utility, so that the teaching of untiring diligence is scarcely heard anymore. If Your Majesty, in following the name, unfailingly demands the reality, and in pondering the beginning, unfailingly enriches the end—using the ordering power of utmost sincerity to bring forth the wondrous function of manifestation and concealment—will this not restore human minds and uphold the moral order of the age? Then the efficacy of grasping the true circumstances of people and following the principles of affairs will hardly even need to be mentioned. This is truly the grand strategy for great active striving. As for perceiving the subtle incipient tendencies and being watchful over oneself when alone, these are indeed the methods of entering virtue through utmost sincerity, and are already encompassed within the twelve admonitions for self-vigilance; how would I dare waste words on them!

Your servant, ignorant of taboos, has offended the imperial majesty and is overcome with trembling and terror. Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
臣張嗣修
臣對臣聞帝王繼天而凝命也必主之以無
逸之心而後可以端天下之治本必敦之以
無爲之體而後可以興天下之治功夫所謂
無逸者非徒辨色會盈敝神勞形已也惟存
敬畏之忱懋時幾之敕法天行之剛健而自
强不息者是已所謂無爲者非徒端居玄默
尊嚴若神已也惟總庶政而挈要分衆職以
亮工法天命之於穆而默斡化機者是已主
之以無逸則精神心術日運量于天下而不
===
至有怠忽荒棄之虞敦之以無爲則法制紀
綱日勤施于四方而不見其煩擾更張之迹
由是凝旒端冕萬邦樂奠枕之安畫衣象冠
天下成覆盂之治古之帝王獨觀乎昭曠之
原弘化于穆清之上而中外禔福夷夏咸寧
者隆此道也欽惟
皇帝陛下
英資天啓

translation_en:
Your servant Zhang Sixiu 張嗣修

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when emperors and kings succeed to Heaven and consolidate the Mandate, they must ground themselves in a mind free from idleness before they can rectify the fundamental basis of governance for all under Heaven; and they must cultivate the substance of non-purposive action before they can raise up the achievements of governance for all under Heaven. Now, what is meant by "freedom from idleness" is not merely holding court at daybreak as the hall fills, exhausting one's spirit and wearing out one's body; rather, it is simply preserving a sincere reverence and awe, exerting oneself in timely and subtle admonition, and modeling oneself on the firm vigor of Heaven's movement so as to strive unceasingly. What is meant by "non-purposive action" is not merely sitting upright in mysterious silence, dignified and austere like a spirit; rather, it is simply overseeing the myriad affairs of state while grasping their essentials, dividing offices among the many officials to bring accomplishments to light, and modeling oneself on the profound solemnity of Heaven's Mandate to silently turn the pivot of transformation. When one grounds oneself in freedom from idleness, one's vital spirit and mental craft daily encompass and measure the realm, without any danger of falling into negligence or abandonment; when one cultivates the substance of non-purposive action, laws, institutions, and thethreads of order are daily and diligently applied throughout the four quarters, without leaving any trace of vexatious disturbance or abrupt upheaval. Through this, with pendant beads hanging still on the imperial crown, the myriad states rejoice in the security of a firmly placed pillow; with symbolic punishments of painted garments and figured caps, the realm achieves the stable governance of an upturned bowl. That the emperors and kings of antiquity uniquely contemplated the luminous and vast source, broadened transformation from above in serene purity, and brought about blessed fortune within and without so that both non-Chinese and Chinese enjoyed peace—it was by exalting this Way.

Your servant reverently reflects that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed by Heaven with heroic talent and daily renewing Your sagely learning, has answered the flourishing cycle of five hundred years for true kings and gloriously received the Precious Mandate; succeeding to…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
祖宗億萬年之大統而丕振
瑶圖
明良交泰宫府一體以朝廷則清明矣吏稱民安
遠懷邇悅以中國則順治矣黠虜納貢炎荒
息警以四夷則賓服矣乃猶望道未見進臣
等而策之于
廷慨慕乎虞周之盛治而有歉于理效之罔臻
思所以脩舉之策斯心也不自滿假稽于有
衆之盛心也顧臣伏處草茅未聞
廟堂之鴻議獨挾其芻蕘之陋習何足以塞
===
明詔奉
大對雖然請誦所聞而
陛下試垂聽焉臣聞古之君天下者未有不以憂
勤保之而以逸豫失之者顧有治本焉有治
體焉憂勤惕厲操存匪懈以作其有爲之志
者所謂治本也操執簡要任賢使能以運其
無爲之化者所謂治體也主之無其本則以
簡逸之心懷之于存主之地其弊也將至於
廢弛而不振出之無其體則以操切之念施
之于措畫之間其弊也將至于勞擾而多事

punctuated:
祖宗億萬年之大統，而丕振瑶圖。明良交泰，宫府一體，以朝廷則清明矣；吏稱民安，遠懷邇悅，以中國則順治矣；黠虜納貢，炎荒息警，以四夷則賓服矣。乃猶望道未見，進臣等而策之于廷，慨慕乎虞、周之盛治，而有歉于理效之罔臻，思所以脩舉之策。斯心也，不自滿假，稽于有衆之盛心也。顧臣伏處草茅，未聞廟堂之鴻議，獨挾其芻蕘之陋習，何足以塞明詔、奉大對？雖然，請誦所聞，而陛下試垂聽焉。
臣聞古之君天下者，未有不以憂勤保之，而以逸豫失之者。顧有治本焉，有治體焉。憂勤惕厲，操存匪懈，以作其有爲之志者，所謂治本也；操執簡要，任賢使能，以運其無爲之化者，所謂治體也。主之無其本，則以簡逸之心，懷之于存主之地，其弊也將至於廢弛而不振；出之無其體，則以操切之念，施之于措畫之間，其弊也將至于勞擾而多事。
translation_en:
… the great succession of the Imperial Ancestors for hundreds of millions of years, and gloriously invigorate the precious imperial enterprise. With an enlightened sovereign and virtuous ministers in harmonious communion, and the inner palace and outer court united as one body, as for the court, it is clear and bright; with officials equal to their duties and the people at peace, the distant cherished and the near delighted, as for the Central Realm, it is smoothly governed; with the cunning northern tribes presenting tribute and alarms ceasing in the scorching southern wilds, as for the four border peoples, they have submitted in allegiance. Yet You still gaze toward the Way as though not yet having seen it, calling forward Your servants to question us on policy in the Palace, admiring with deep feeling the flourishing governance of Yu [Shun] and Zhou while feeling dissatisfied that the effects of good order have not yet been fully reached, and pondering the policies by which to restore and elevate them. This mind is the grand mind that does not grow self-satisfied, but consults the multitude. Yet Your servant has lived in obscurity among the thatch and reeds and has not heard the grand deliberations of the court; holding only to the crude habits of a grass-cutter and firewood-gatherer, how could I suffice to fulfill Your luminous edict and offer a great reply? Even so, allow me to recite what I have heard, and may Your Majesty deign to listen.

Your servant has heard that among those in antiquity who ruled the world as sovereigns, there was never one who did not preserve it through anxious diligence and lose it through idle indulgence. Yet there is the root of governance, and there is the body of governance. To be anxiously diligent and vigilantly alert, holding fast to one's mind without laxity so as to rouse the will for active achievement—this is what is called the root of governance. To hold to what is simple and essential, employing the worthy and commissioning the capable so as to set in motion the transformation of non-purposive action—this is what is called the body of governance. If in presiding over it one lacks its root, then one harbors a mind of simplistic ease in the seat of inner mastery, and the resulting abuse will reach the point of neglect and laxity without vigor; if in issuing it forth one lacks its body, then one applies thoughts of harsh urgency in the midst of planning and execution, and the resulting abuse will reach the point of exhausting disturbance and excessive meddling.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
不觀之天乎今夫天運而不積健而有常一
元之運亘萬古而不息者天之所以主宰化
原也分之以四時布之以五氣鼓之以風霆
熯之以日月潤之以雨露肅之以雪霜百神
受命而羣動咸理者天之所以斡運化權也
何者天以神用而不以形用者也惟其以神
用也故品彙咸章而莫非其化醇之妙惟其
不以形用也故庶物咸若而不見其作爲之
勞此天之所以爲大也觀天則知君道矣聖
人者法天之健以端其本而存之以匪懈之
===
心法天之化以立其體而操之以不煩之術
故不見而章不動而變無爲而成也書曰惟
天聰明惟聖時憲憲天者憲以此而已古之
聖帝能憲天者莫過于虞舜矣時幾以敕天
命兢業以圖萬幾推其心何敢一時而少懈
者及考其治亦曰疇咨四岳明目達聰而已
固未嘗煩擾焦勞而身親百工之事也是以
六府孔脩四方風動恭已而天下治焉古之
聖王能憲天者莫過于周文矣日昃而不遑
食惠鮮以和萬民推其心何敢一時而少懈

punctuated: 不觀之天乎？今夫天，運而不積，健而有常，一元之運，亘萬古而不息者，天之所以主宰化原也；分之以四時，布之以五氣，鼓之以風霆，熯之以日月，潤之以雨露，肅之以雪霜，百神受命而羣動咸理者，天之所以斡運化權也。何者？天以神用，而不以形用者也。惟其以神用也，故品彙咸章，而莫非其化醇之妙；惟其不以形用也，故庶物咸若，而不見其作爲之勞。此天之所以爲大也。觀天則知君道矣。聖人者，法天之健以端其本，而存之以匪懈之心；法天之化以立其體，而操之以不煩之術。故不見而章，不動而變，無爲而成也。《書》曰：「惟天聰明，惟聖時憲。」憲天者，憲以此而已。古之聖帝能憲天者，莫過于虞舜矣。時幾以敕天命，兢業以圖萬幾，推其心，何敢一時而少懈者？及考其治，亦曰疇咨四岳、明目達聰而已，固未嘗煩擾焦勞，而身親百工之事也。是以六府孔脩，四方風動，恭已而天下治焉。古之聖王能憲天者，莫過于周文矣。日昃而不遑食，惠鮮以和萬民，推其心，何敢一時而少懈
translation_en: Have you not observed Heaven? Now, Heaven revolves without accumulating, and is vigorous and constant. That the movement of the primal pneuma extends through all antiquity without ceasing is how Heaven presides over the source of transformation. Dividing it by the four seasons, spreading it through the five phases of qi, rousing it with wind and thunder, warming it with the sun and moon, moistening it with rain and dew, and making it austere with snow and frost, so that the hundred spirits receive its command and the myriad living things are all put in order—this is how Heaven turns and wields the authority of transformation. Why is this? Because Heaven operates through spirit and not through physical form. Precisely because it operates through spirit, the myriad categories of beings all become manifest, and nothing is outside the marvel of its generative perfection; precisely because it does not operate through physical form, the multitude of things all conform to their nature, yet one never sees the toil of its deliberate action. This is why Heaven is great. By observing Heaven, one knows the Way of the ruler. The sage models himself on the vigor of Heaven to rectify his foundation, preserving it with an unremitting mind; he models himself on the transformation of Heaven to establish his governance in practice, wielding it through an unvexed method. Therefore, without showing himself he becomes manifest, without moving he transforms, and without deliberate action he brings things to completion. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Only Heaven is all-intelligent and all-discerning; only the sage models himself on it." To model oneself on Heaven is simply to model oneself on this. Among the sage-emperors of antiquity who were able to model themselves on Heaven, none surpassed Shun of Yu (Yu Shun 虞舜). At every moment and subtle incipience he was cautious of Heaven's Mandate, and with fear and trembling he attended to the myriad affairs of state; if we examine his mind, how would he dare to relax even slightly for a single moment? Yet when we examine his governance, it consisted simply of consulting the Four Peaks (Siyue) and seeing and hearing clearly with the eyes and ears of the empire; he certainly never busied or exhausted himself with petty vexations by personally handling the tasks of the hundred officials. Therefore, the six treasuries of nature were well-ordered, the four quarters were moved as by the wind, and by merely holding himself in reverence the empire was well-governed. Among the sage-kings of antiquity who were able to model themselves on Heaven, none surpassed King Wen of Zhou (Zhou Wen 周文). From morning until the sun inclined to the west he had no leisure to eat, showing kindness to the destitute and solitary so as to harmonize the myriad people; if we examine his mind, how would he dare to relax even slightly for a single moment…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
者及考其治亦曰三宅三俊克知灼見而已
固未甞苛察瑣屑而兼獄愼之煩也是以西
土怙冒有夏脩和不顯而厥命新焉蓋有舜
之兢業文之不遑則雖端委九重聲色不動
而精神之所灌注自不至于偷惰以隳事幾
無爲也而無不爲也有舜之恭已文之罔知
則雖率作興事奔走羣工而綱領之所提挈
自不至于紛擾以紊事理有爲也而實無爲
也迨後世憲天之學不明君人之道未講彼
以逸豫滅德者無以議爲矣間有志于是者
===
則又倒行而逆施之唐玄宗以天下之政付
姚崇至奏選除則仰觀殿屋自以爲知大體
矣然荒淫自恣大柄下移釀成幸蜀之禍舜
之無爲文之罔知者顧如是耶隋文帝日親
庶政衞士傳餐自以爲能勵精矣然任數以
馭下苛察以炫明至使人遺吏以賄而罪之
乃一傳而國失舜之兢業文之不遑者顧如
是耶無爲也而必若玄宗適足以致亂而已
有爲也而必若隋文適足以致亡而已故臣
以爲舛也恭惟我

… Yet when we examine his governance, it is simply said that "as to the three grades of office and the three categories of able men, he was able to know them and see them clearly." Indeed, he never engaged in harsh scrutiny or petty details, nor took upon himself the trouble of judicial cautions. Therefore, the western lands relied upon his sheltering care, the realm of Xia was brought into order and harmony, and though his virtue was unostentatious, his Mandate was made new. For if a ruler possesses the cautious diligence of Shun and the tireless industry of King Wen, then even though he sits in ceremonial robes within the ninefold palace without altering his voice or countenance, the infusion of his vital spirit naturally prevents any slackness or indolence that would ruin crucial affairs: this is non-action (wuwei), yet nothing is left undone. And if he possesses the reverent self-restraint of Shun and the deliberate non-interference of King Wen, then even though he leads the initiation of enterprises and sets all the officials in motion, his grasp of the essential guiding principles naturally prevents any confusion or meddling that would disorder the pattern of affairs: this is action (youwei), yet in reality it is non-action.

When it came to later ages, the learning of modeling oneself on Heaven was obscured and the Way of ruling men went undiscussed. Those who destroyed their virtue through ease and pleasure are beneath discussion. Occasionally there were rulers who aspired to this ideal, yet they acted perversely and applied it backwards. Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang entrusted the governance of the empire to Yao Chong; when memorials on official selections and appointments were presented, he merely gazed up at the palace roof, fancying that he understood the grand principles of rule. Yet he indulged himself in dissipation and license, supreme authority shifted downward, and this brewed the disaster of his flight to Shu. Was the non-action of Shun or the non-interference of King Wen really like this? Emperor Wen of the Sui personally attended to myriad administrative affairs every day, having the palace guards pass in his meals, and fancied himself capable of vigorous diligence. Yet he relied on manipulative artifice to control his subordinates and used harsh scrutiny to show off his discernment, even going so far as to send people to offer bribes to officials in order to convict them—and after a single transmission of the throne, the state was lost. Was the cautious diligence of Shun or the tireless industry of King Wen really like this? To practice non-action in the manner of Xuanzong is just enough to bring about disorder; to practice action in the manner of Emperor Wen of the Sui is just enough to bring about ruin. Therefore your servant considers them misguided.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
太祖高皇帝
天錫智勇再造乾坤
神功聖德有亘古而莫之與儷者然猶孜孜為治
罔敢自逸伏讀
祖訓有曰晚眠早起勞心焦思惟恐萬幾之不理
是心也即舜兢業文不遑之心也然當是時
元功佐命則徐常之倫宣其威帷幄運籌則
劉李之儔賛其畫文學則葉章桂宋治民則
陶黃郁開斯亦當時五臣四友之朋已又嘗
諭侍臣曰人君固貴明斷然不可煩苛見或未至
===
則損人君之明過察則失人君之量是心也即
舜恭已文罔知之心也是以智勇輻輳羣策
畢舉興造鴻業身致太平自天地剖判以來
未有二此者也謂非主之以無逸運之以無
為曷以臻茲乎仰惟
陛下臨御以來孜孜圖治
經筵講讀不輟于暑寒章疏省覽無間於朝夕
因災警戒則懸牌以代瞽史之規
聽講寶箴則拱立以
納輔臣之誨以立治本則我

punctuated:
太祖高皇帝天錫智勇，再造乾坤，神功聖德，有亘古而莫之與儷者。然猶孜孜為治，罔敢自逸。伏讀《祖訓》，有曰：「晚眠早起，勞心焦思，惟恐萬幾之不理。」是心也，即舜兢業、文不遑之心也。然當是時，元功佐命，則徐、常之倫宣其威；帷幄運籌，則劉、李之儔賛其畫；文學，則葉、章、桂、宋；治民，則陶、黃、郁、開，斯亦當時五臣、四友之朋已。又嘗諭侍臣曰：「人君固貴明斷，然不可煩苛。見或未至，則損人君之明；過察，則失人君之量。」是心也，即舜恭已、文罔知之心也。是以智勇輻輳，羣策畢舉，興造鴻業，身致太平，自天地剖判以來，未有二此者也。謂非主之以無逸、運之以無為，曷以臻茲乎？

translation_en:
…Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), was endowed by Heaven with wisdom and valor, remaking heaven and earth. His divine achievements and sagely virtue have been unmatched throughout all antiquity. Yet he still laboured tirelessly at governance, never daring to indulge in ease. Humbly reading the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun), there are the words: "Retiring late and rising early, toiling in heart and anxious in thought, fearing only that the myriad affairs of state might go unattended." This mind is none other than the cautious and reverent mind of Shun, and the mind of King Wen that allowed no leisure for meals. Yet at that time, among those of primary merit who aided the Mandate, peers like Xu [Da 徐達] and Chang [Yuchun 常遇春] projected his martial awe; in devising strategies within the command tent, fellows like Liu [Ji 劉基] and Li [Shanchang 李善長] assisted his plans; in literature and learning, there were Ye [Chen 葉琛], Zhang [Yi 章溢], Gui [Yanliang 桂彥良], and Song [Lian 宋濂]; in governing the people, there were Tao [An 陶安], Huang [Gu 黃觀 / 黃哲?], Yu [Xin 郁新], and Kai [Ji 開濟]. These were indeed the equals of Shun's five ministers and King Wen's four friends in their own day. He also once instructed his attending ministers, saying: "A ruler certainly values clear decisiveness, yet he must not be petty or harsh. If his perception falls short, it impairs the ruler's clarity; if he is overly scrutinizing, it forfeits the ruler's magnanimity." This mind is none other than the mind of Shun holding himself in reverence, and of King Wen taking no cognizance of details. Therefore, wisdom and bravery converged like spokes at a hub, all plans were fully enacted, he founded a grand enterprise, and personally brought about great peace—since the separation of heaven and earth, there has never been a second to this. If one were to say this was not presided over through untiring diligence and operated through non-purposive action (wuwei), how else could such a state have been attained?

Looking up in reflection, since Your Majesty ascended the throne, You have laboured tirelessly to plan for good governance: lectures and readings at the Classics Colloquium (jingyan) have not ceased in summer heat or winter cold; the inspection and perusal of memorials have continued without interruption morning and evening; taking warning from natural disasters, You hung plaques to serve in place of the admonitions of blind musicians and scribes; listening to lectures on precious admonitions, You stood with hands folded in reverence to accept the instructions of the Grand Secretaries. title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
聖祖晩眠早起憂勤萬幾之心也簡賢任能而分
以衆理之職考言詢事而馭以賞罰之權以
立治體則我
聖祖驅策羣才提挈綱要之軌也宜其百工勵翼
庶績咸舉矣臣伏讀
聖策猶以帑庾之未充民生之未遂吏治之罔宣
武備之靡振欿然有所未愜於衷者豈奉行
德意者或未之至乎無亦
陛下之兢惕或未能如古帝王之懇切而政要所
在或未能如古帝王之審識乎臣聞天下之
===
事有本有末有要有詳本在於上末在於下
要在於主詳在於臣故主好要則百事詳主
好詳則百事荒是以明君之理天下無庸自
以爲也任人而已
陛下如欲足財則胡不擇羣臣中練於綜理者而
使之爲司計如欲民安則胡不擇羣臣中長
於治民者而付之以司牧如欲興吏治則胡
不擇羣臣之精於衡鑑者而責之以秉銓如
欲足兵則胡不擇羣臣之嫻於軍旅者而畀
之以治戎既得其人因詢之曰倉庾多匱云

punctuated: 聖祖晩眠早起、憂勤萬幾之心也。簡賢任能，而分以衆理之職；考言詢事，而馭以賞罰之權。以立治體，則我聖祖驅策羣才、提挈綱要之軌也。宜其百工勵翼，庶績咸舉矣。臣伏讀聖策，猶以帑庾之未充、民生之未遂、吏治之罔宣、武備之靡振，欿然有所未愜於衷者。豈奉行德意者或未之至乎？無亦陛下之兢惕，或未能如古帝王之懇切；而政要所在，或未能如古帝王之審識乎？臣聞天下之事，有本有末，有要有詳。本在於上，末在於下；要在於主，詳在於臣。故主好要則百事詳，主好詳則百事荒。是以明君之理天下，無庸自以爲也，任人而已。陛下如欲足財，則胡不擇羣臣中練於綜理者，而使之爲司計？如欲民安，則胡不擇羣臣中長於治民者，而付之以司牧？如欲興吏治，則胡不擇羣臣之精於衡鑑者，而責之以秉銓？如欲足兵，則胡不擇羣臣之嫻於軍旅者，而畀之以治戎？既得其人，因詢之曰：倉庾多匱，云
translation_en:
… the mind of our Sacred Ancestor, who retired late and rose early, anxiously and diligently attending to the myriad affairs of state. Selecting the worthy and employing the capable, and dividing among them the duties of collective administration; examining their words and inquiring into their deeds, and governing them with the authority of rewards and punishments—in establishing the framework of governance, this follows the model of our Sacred Ancestor inmarshaling all talents and grasping the essential principles. It is fitting that all officials exert themselves in reverent assistance and that all state enterprises are fully carried out. Yet, as your servant humbly reads the Sacred Policy Question, Your Majesty still feels dissatisfied at heart because the treasuries and granaries are not yet full, the people's livelihoods are not yet secure, official administration is not yet effective, and military preparedness is not yet invigorated. Could it be that those who carry out Your Majesty's virtuous intentions have not done so to the utmost? Or is it rather that Your Majesty's cautious vigilance is perhaps not yet as earnest as that of the ancient emperors and kings, and that Your discernment of where the essentials of governance lie is perhaps not yet as penetrating as theirs?

Your servant has heard that in the affairs of the world, there are roots and branches, essentials and details. The roots lie above, while the branches lie below; the essentials rest with the ruler, while the details rest with the ministers. Therefore, if the ruler attends to the essentials, the hundred affairs will be handled in full detail; if the ruler busies himself with the details, the hundred affairs will fall into neglect. Thus, when an enlightened ruler governs the empire, there is no need for him to do everything himself; he simply entrusts responsibilities to the right men. If Your Majesty wishes to make wealth sufficient, why not select from among the officials those skilled in comprehensive management and appoint them to take charge of fiscal administration? If You wish the people to be at peace, why not select from among the officials those adept at governing the people and entrust them with the duties of local pastors? If You wish to invigorate official administration, why not select from among the officials those discerning in the evaluation of men and charge them with holding the scales of personnel selection? If You wish to make the military sufficient, why not select from among the officials those well-versed in military affairs and assign them to manage the armed forces? Having obtained the right men, You should then inquire of them, saying: "The granaries and storehouses are largely depleted; how …"

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
何而充之民生未遂云何而安之吏不稱職
云何而興之戎伍多缺云何而實之云何而
破拘攣之議云何而去文冒之習因以其言
而任之事即以其事而責之成竅言而無當
者却之虚稱而無用者去之聲實不眩於前
而賞罰必信於後則羣臣莫不畢智竭能以
任上之事而百務舉矣何必膠膠擾擾勞形
苦體以侵百工之事乎故曰主術約而易操
也雖然猶末也今夫人之一身視則以目聽
則以耳持行則以手足主之者心也非吾之
===
心日惺惺焉以為之君則耳目四體罔攸稟
令而不得以各效其能又譬之治家者總之
以家相分之以衆子耕則問奴織則問婢而
為之主人者亦必早作而晏息日省而月試
而後子弟僕婢不敢怠荒而疾趨其事斯家
之所以成也故君者心也主人也臣耳目四
體也子弟僕婢也
陛下既已得四者之人而任之矣尤必倡之以明
作之念主之以勵精之心財賦之任責之計
曹而躬行儉德以率先之者不敢懈也司牧

而後子弟僕婢不敢怠荒而疾趨其事斯家
之所以成也故君者心也主人也臣耳目四
體也子弟僕婢也
陛下既已得四者之人而任之矣尤必倡之以明
作之念主之以勵精之心財賦之任責之計
曹而躬行儉德以率先之者不敢懈也司牧
punctuated: 何而充之？民生未遂，云何而安之？吏不稱職，云何而興之？戎伍多缺，云何而實之？云何而破拘攣之議？云何而去文冒之習？」因以其言而任之事，即以其事而責之成。竅言而無當者却之，虚稱而無用者去之。聲實不眩於前，而賞罰必信於後，則羣臣莫不畢智竭能以任上之事，而百務舉矣！何必膠膠擾擾、勞形苦體，以侵百工之事乎？故曰：「主術約而易操也。」雖然，猶末也。今夫人之一身，視則以目，聽則以耳，持行則以手足，主之者心也。非吾之心日惺惺焉以為之君，則耳目四體罔攸稟令，而不得以各效其能。又譬之治家者，總之以家相，分之以衆子，耕則問奴，織則問婢，而為之主人者，亦必早作而晏息，日省而月試，而後子弟僕婢不敢怠荒而疾趨其事，斯家之所以成也。故君者，心也，主人也；臣，耳目四體也，子弟僕婢也。陛下既已得四者之人而任之矣，尤必倡之以明作之念，主之以勵精之心。財賦之任責之計曹，而躬行儉德以率先之者不敢懈也；司牧
