…how to replenish them? The people's livelihood is not yet secure; how to give them peace? Officials are not equal to their offices; how to rouse them? The military ranks have many vacancies; how to fill them? How to break through hidebound deliberations? How to rid ourselves of the habit of superficiality and false pretenses?" Then, on the basis of their words, entrust them with the tasks, and by means of those very tasks, hold them responsible for results. Reject those who offer empty words [?] without substance, and dismiss those who enjoy hollow reputations without practical use. If reputation and reality do not confuse you beforehand, and rewards and punishments are unfailingly trustworthy afterward, then none among the body of officials will fail to exhaust their wisdom and strength in undertaking the sovereign's affairs, and all tasks will be accomplished! Why must one be bogged down in fuss and bother, wearing out one's form and exhausting one's body in order to usurp the duties of the various officials? Therefore it is said: "The art of the ruler is concise and easy to wield."

Even so, this is still secondary. Now, as for a person's body: for seeing one uses the eyes, for hearing one uses the ears, and for grasping and walking one uses the hands and feet, while that which rules over them is the mind. Unless one's own mind remains ever alert each day to act as their sovereign, the ears, eyes, and four limbs will have nowhere from which to receive commands, and will be unable to render their respective capacities. Take another analogy, that of managing a household: one oversees it as a whole through a household steward, divides the duties among the various sons, asks the male servants about plowing, and asks the female servants about weaving. Yet the one who is master of the house must also rise early and retire late, inspecting daily and testing monthly; only then will the sons, younger brothers, and male and female servants not dare to be lazy or neglectful, hurrying instead to their tasks—and this is how a household is established. Therefore, the ruler is the mind and the master of the house; the ministers are the ears, eyes, and four limbs, the sons, younger brothers, and male and female servants.

Since Your Majesty has already found men for these four responsibilities and entrusted them with office, You must all the more lead them with a resolve for enlightened action and preside over them with a mind of vigorous dedication. text:
之任責之守令而惠鮮懷保以圖慮之者不
敢懈也辨官之任責之司銓而闢門側席以
旁求之者不敢懈也治戎之任責之司馬而
居安慮危以振飭之者不敢懈也夫鼓宮而
宮動鼓角而角應其理自然也
陛下之臣見上之加意如此上之精勵如此又孰
不思畢智竭力各效其能以順上之指乎若
是則四者之效
陛下皆可以坐而致之譬之紫樞奠位而萬象咸
拱玄工冥運而四敘成功斯理道之至極也
===
是之謂以無逸之心而行無為之事故治定
之後人見夫庶政惟和萬方承式莫不曰此
真大有為之君也而不知其有為者本于無
為者也人見夫聲色不動指顧不煩莫不曰
此上古無為之治也而不知其無為者成于
有為者也有為者精明之治功無為者惇大
之治體信有如
聖制所謂其道相須者也乃今議者不稱舜之兢
業而稱舜之無為不稱文王之日昃而稱文
王之罔兼不稱聖帝顯王之大有為而稱王

Now, when one strikes the gong note, the gong string vibrates, and when one strikes the jue note, the jue string responds; this principle is completely natural. When Your Majesty's ministers see the Sovereign paying such close attention and exerting such vigorous diligence, who among them would not think to exhaust his wisdom and strength, each offering his abilities in order to comply with the Sovereign's aims? If this is so, then the efficacy of these four matters can all be achieved by Your Majesty while sitting in repose. It is like the Pole Star fixed in its place while all the myriad phenomena bow toward it, or the mysterious artificer of heaven operating unseen while the four seasons bring their work to completion—this is the ultimate perfection of the Way of governance. This is what is meant by carrying out the affairs of non-action with a mind that knows no indolence. Therefore, once order is established, when people see all governmental affairs in harmony and the myriad regions taking them as their model, none will fail to say, "This is truly a sovereign of great purposeful action!"—not knowing that his purposeful action is rooted in non-action. And when people see that neither voice nor countenance is stirred, and neither pointing nor looking about requires trouble, none will fail to say, "This is the governance of non-action of high antiquity!"—not knowing that his non-action is brought to completion through purposeful action. Purposeful action is the lucid and discerning achievement of governance; non-action is the generous and magnanimous substance of governance. Truly it is just as Your Majesty's Sacred Decree states: "Their Ways are mutually dependent." text:
臣曾朝節
臣對臣聞帝王之恢鴻業經遠猷也固必爲
天下持不自逸之心而後有以握出治之本
尤必爲天下擴不自用之公而後有以收致
治之效夫天下之大四海之廣皆於人君乎
統理之則雖欲以一日晏然於民上有不可
得者故其兢兢然日以其治圖惟於心而不
敢以自逸所以爲天下端治本也然人君之
尊亦一人之身也如必事事而親之則雖帝
王之縱於天者固有餘智安所爲而不效而
===

終阻於勢之弗周明君審於治體當不若是
其自勞瘁爲也於是乎以其不自逸之心擴
之爲不自用之公以天下之事付天下之人
治之以天下之才爲天下之人用之意念常
宅於憂勤而形常不勞精神常流於寰宇而
氣常自定故天下見人君日黽勉於上而終
無以窺其作爲之迹人君與天下相忘於無
爲而初不見其有因循頽惰之弊此之謂無
爲而無不爲而恭己成功之要術也夫苟不

臣對：臣聞帝王之恢鴻業、經遠猷也，固必爲天下持不自逸之心，而後有以握出治之本；尤必爲天下擴不自用之公，而後有以收致治之效。夫天下之大，四海之廣，皆於人君乎統理之，則雖欲以一日晏然於民上，有不可得者。故其兢兢然日以其治圖惟於心，而不敢以自逸，所以爲天下端治本也。然人君之尊，亦一人之身也。如必事事而親之，則雖帝王之縱於天者固有餘智，安所爲而不效，而聰明容有未逮，心思容有未及，則求治之切，終阻於勢之弗周。明君審於治體，當不若是其自勞瘁爲也。於是乎以其不自逸之心，擴之爲不自用之公，以天下之事付天下之人治之，以天下之才爲天下之人用之。意念常宅於憂勤，而形常不勞；精神常流於寰宇，而氣常自定。故天下見人君日黽勉於上，而終無以窺其作爲之迹；人君與天下相忘於無爲，而初不見其有因循頽惰之弊。此之謂無爲而無不爲，而恭己成功之要術也。夫苟不
translation_en:
Your servant Zeng Chaojie 曾朝節.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when emperors and kings expand their grand enterprise and plan their far-reaching counsels, they must certainly maintain on behalf of the realm a mind that does not indulge in self-ease, and only then have the means to grasp the foundation from which good governance springs; even more so must they broaden on behalf of the realm an impartiality that does not rely solely on oneself, and only then have the means to reap the results of bringing about good order. Now, given the vastness of the realm and the breadth of the Four Seas, all of which are unified and regulated by the ruler of men, even if he wished to rest comfortably above the people for a single day, it would be impossible to do so. Therefore, he is cautiously and apprehensionally pondering governance in his mind day by day, not daring to indulge in self-ease; this is how he rectifies the foundation of governance for the realm. Yet the exalted ruler of men is still only the body of a single person. If he must attend to every matter in person, then even though emperors and kings endowed by Heaven certainly possess surplus wisdom—and what might they undertake without effect?—their keenness of hearing and sight may still fail to reach everything, and their thoughts and reflections may still fail to extend everywhere; thus their earnest desire for good governance will ultimately be hindered by the impossibility of covering all circumstances. An enlightened ruler who understands the essentials of governance should not exhaust himself in such a manner. Thereupon, he takes his mind that does not indulge in self-ease and broadens it into an impartiality that does not rely solely on oneself, entrusting the affairs of the realm to the people of the realm to govern, and employing the talents of the realm for the sake of the people of the realm. His thoughts and intentions constantly dwell in anxious diligence, yet his physical form is constantly unwearied; his vital spirit constantly flows throughout the universe, yet hisvital energy remains constantly composed. Therefore, the realm sees the ruler of men striving diligently above day after day, yet ultimately has no way to spy out the traces of his deliberate action; the ruler of men and the realm forget each other in non-action, yet from the beginning one sees no flaw of passive routine or laxity. This is what is meant by doing nothing and yet leaving nothing undone, and it is the essential art of achieving success while remaining reverently self-possessed. Now if one does not…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
繇是道撫天下之大業而容有一毫自逸之
心是以無心棄天下也固非人君之所以圖
治也操此心之無逸而或有一毫自用之心
是以有心擾天下也亦非人君之所以圖治
也蓋臣伏在草野涵泳
聖化則嘗究極古今之成迹商諏治理之大原竊
以為人君之所以撫運握圖統一區內雖其
綜緝庶務調劑羣品其道非一端要之惟不
自逸與不自用之二言或者其足以仰裨
聖治之萬一矣玆者臣叨與有司之薦獲奉
===
大對顧何敢不盡其愚謹因
聖問所及而詳陳之惟
陛下垂聽焉伏惟
陛下以
聰明神聖之資而履
純熈昌明之祚以
剛健中正之德而擴統馭齊一之規蓋天縱之
以為
君師使出而繼虞周之芳軌纘帝王之懿休也其
於治理之所以得失古今之所以隆替固已

… follow this Way. To preside over the great enterprise of the empire while allowing even the slightest mind toward self-indulgence is to abandon the empire through heedlessness—this is certainly not how a ruler plans for good governance. Conversely, to hold fast to a mind free of self-indulgence while harboring even the slightest mind toward self-reliance is to throw the empire into confusion through willful interference—nor is this how a ruler plans for good governance. When your servant lived in obscurity in the countryside, steeped in Your Sacred transforming influence, I once thoroughly investigated the established traces of antiquity and the present and deliberated upon the great foundations of the principles of governance. I venture to believe that in a ruler's presiding over his destined era, grasping the imperial chart, and unifying all within the realm, although his ways of weaving together the myriad affairs of state and harmonizing the multitude of officials are not confined to a single method, in sum, these two phrases alone—"not indulging oneself" and "not relying solely on oneself"—may perhaps suffice to offer a ten-thousandth part of assistance to Your Sacred governance. Now, having been unworthy to receive the recommendation of the authorities and privileged to offer this grand reply, how could I dare not pour forth the entirety of my humble thoughts! I respectfully set them forth in detail in accordance with what Your Sacred inquiry has touched upon, and pray only that Your Majesty deign to listen.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
燭照而洞察之矣乃玆拳拳求虞周之所以
致治此聖不自聖之心也臣俯思之隆古之
治必徵之詩書而詩書所稱則虞周其獨盛
也已然虞周之盛臣得之於誦讀想像切矣
思以親履其庭觀其所謂盛而不可得也今
陛下躬聖德建至治不啻虞周矣伏讀
聖制猶曰朕甚嘉之慕之蓋毅然以舜文自期使
臣曩時所誦讀想像者得親觀其盛也臣敢
稱引詩書以舜文所以造虞周之治者先為
陛下述之舜之受終文祖紹堯致治也在璣衡而
===
七政齊敘百揆而庶尹諧木金水火土穀則
時序而六府修矣利用厚生正德則底績而
三事治矣舜之所以治虞者何盛也文之修
和有夏丕冒下土也以咸德肇造邦家而咸
寧四海以謨烈啓佑孫子而咸正靡缺禮備
樂和而道化其旁洽矣刑修政舉而法守其
畫一矣文之所以造周者何盛也然舜之所
以治虞固非曰虞當中天之運聽氣化之自
盛而無所用心也不曰舜兢業萬幾乎而其
所以兢業云者則亦持其大體屢省乃成而

punctuated: 燭照而洞察之矣。乃玆拳拳求虞、周之所以致治，此聖不自聖之心也。臣俯思之：隆古之治，必徵之《詩》、《書》；而《詩》、《書》所稱，則虞、周其獨盛也已。然虞、周之盛，臣得之於誦讀，想像切矣，思以親履其庭、觀其所謂盛，而不可得也。今陛下躬聖德、建至治，不啻虞、周矣。伏讀聖制，猶曰「朕甚嘉之慕之」，蓋毅然以舜、文自期，使臣曩時所誦讀想像者，得親觀其盛也。臣敢稱引《詩》、《書》，以舜、文所以造虞、周之治者，先為陛下述之。舜之受終文祖，紹堯致治也，在璣衡而七政齊，敘百揆而庶尹諧；木、金、水、火、土、穀，則時序而六府修矣；利用、厚生、正德，則底績而三事治矣。舜之所以治虞者，何盛也！文之修和有夏，丕冒下土也，以咸德肇造邦家，而咸寧四海；以謨烈啓佑孫子，而咸正靡缺；禮備樂和，而道化其旁洽矣；刑修政舉，而法守其畫一矣。文之所以造周者，何盛也！然舜之所以治虞，固非曰虞當中天之運，聽氣化之自盛，而無所用心也。不曰舜兢業萬幾乎？而其所以兢業云者，則亦持其大體，屢省乃成而
translation_en:
…illuminated them like a torch and perceived them thoroughly. Yet now you earnestly seek the means by which Yu and Zhou achieved good governance—this is the mind of a sage who does not consider himself a sage. Your servant has humbly reflected upon this: the governance of high antiquity must be verified through the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu); and among what is praised in the Odes and Documents, Yu and Zhou alone were uniquely flourishing. Yet as for the flourishing of Yu and Zhou, your servant only acquired knowledge of it through recitation and reading, imagining it vividly, and longed to personally tread their courts and witness their so-called flourishing, though that was impossible to attain. Now Your Majesty personally embodies sagely virtue and establishes supreme governance, no less than Yu and Zhou. Humbly reading the Imperial question, you still say, "We greatly praise and admire them," resolutely holding Yourself to the standard of Shun and King Wen, thereby allowing your servant to personally witness today the flourishing that he formerly could only recite, read about, and imagine. Your servant ventures to cite the Odes and Documents to first recount for Your Majesty the means by which Shun and King Wen created the governance of Yu and Zhou.

When Shun received the abdication at the temple of the Accomplished Ancestor and succeeded Yao in achieving good governance, he examined the jade-adorned sighting tube and the seven astronomical regulators were aligned; he ordered the General Regulators and the various officials were harmonized. Wood, metal, water, fire, earth, and grain were seasonally ordered, and thus the Six Treasuries were well maintained; practical use, enrichment of livelihood, and rectification of virtue were brought to fruition, and thus the Three Affairs were well governed. How flourishing were the means by which Shun governed Yu! When King Wen cultivated harmony throughout the realm of Xia and grandly overspread the lands below, through universal virtue he founded the state and brought universal peace to the Four Seas; through his plans and achievements he enlightened and aided his descendants, so that all was rectified without deficiency. Rituals were complete and music was harmonious, so moral transformation spread widely; punishments were regulated and administration was upheld, so the observance of laws was uniform. How flourishing were the means by which King Wen created Zhou! Yet the means by which Shun governed Yu certainly did not consist in saying that Yu stood at the zenith of cosmic fortune, leaving the vital transformations to flourish of their own accord without applying his mind to them. Is it not said that Shun attended with cautious diligence to the myriad affairs of state? And what is meant by his cautious diligence is simply that he upheld the great essentials and repeatedly inspected accomplishments…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
巳矣不然舜雖濬哲文明主也然七政之所
以齊庶尹之所以諧六府三事之所以修且
治豈皆無藉於五臣耶使舜而不以付之五
臣是舜特自役其聰明以屑屑於庶物之間
臣未見舜之能爲虞也文之所以造周固非
曰文承世德之後任治運之自昌而無事焦
勞也不曰自朝至于日中昃不遑暇食乎而
其所以不遑云者則亦總攬大綱依其在京
而已矣不然文雖緝熈宣哲主也然謨之所
以顯烈之所以揚禮樂刑政之所以煥然豈
===
誠無資於四友耶使文而不以任之四友是
文特自逞其私智以矻矻於衆務之蹟臣未
見文之能爲周也故書稱庶獄庶慎文王罔
兼而孔子復謂舜無爲而治蓋罔兼者乃其
所以能兼庶物也無爲者乃其所以能運有
爲也是故帝王之於天下惟恃其有不敢自
逸之心而已矣而自逸則幾於廢亦惟恃其
有不敢自用之心而已矣而自用則幾於勞
不自逸之心與不自用之心有以並行而不
悖以其不自逸者責治於心以其不自用者

…and nothing more. Otherwise, although Shun was a ruler of profound wisdom and civilized brightness, how could the ordering of the Seven Directors [sun, moon, and five planets], the harmonizing of the百 various officials, and the repairing and governing of the Six Treasuries and Three Businesses all have been accomplished without relying on his five ministers? Had Shun not entrusted these matters to his five ministers, he would merely have been enslaving his own intelligence to busy himself with petty details among the myriad affairs, and your servant cannot see how Shun could have made the Yu dynasty what it was.

As for the way King Wen founded the Zhou, it was certainly not that, having inherited accumulated virtue from previous generations, he simply left the burgeoning cycle of good rule to flourish on its own without any anxious toil. Is it not said that "from morning to midday and until the sun declined, he did not allow himself leisure to eat"? Yet what is meant by his allowing himself no leisure was simply that he held overall control of the grand outlines while abiding tranquilly in his capital, and nothing more. Otherwise, although King Wen was a ruler of continuing brightness and far-reaching wisdom, how could the manifestation of his counsels, the exaltation of his achievements, and the brilliant flourishing of rites, music, punishments, and administration truly have been achieved without the aid of his Four Friends? Had King Wen not delegated responsibilities to his Four Friends, he would merely have been indulging his private cleverness to toil away at the traces of a multitude of affairs, and your servant cannot see how King Wen could have made the Zhou dynasty what it was.

Therefore, the Book of Documents praises King Wen by saying, "Regarding the numerous lawsuits and numerous precautions, King Wen did not try to encompass them all himself," while Confucius again spoke of Shun as "governing by non-action." Indeed, not trying to encompass everything oneself is precisely how one is able to encompass the myriad affairs; non-action is precisely how one is able to set purposeful action in motion.

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
責治於人有以兼舉而不偏信乎帝之所以
帝與王之所以王其率遵是道也已後之爲
治者不曰我爲萬乘主吾固無以桎梏爲也
則曰天下固莫巳若而必自親事也故荒淫
慆慢者旣以基禍自作聰明者亦以釀亂尚
奚論哉仰惟我
太祖高皇帝
獨稟全智創造區宇是以虞周之聖履虞周之
統也而其所以因事立法酌時定制者綱舉
而目張周慮而曲防博大詳密用以綿十萬
===
億無疆之祚卓乎虞周之再覩而
聖子神孫所當世守也已然其所以致此者則以
其功雖無兢而心恒不自逸智雖如神而才
恒不自用故自御曆以來三十餘年早朝晏
罷未嘗時刻少怠信有如
聖制之所述矣然當時名卿碩輔濟濟布列有若
劉基宋濂王禕陶安若而人相與諮謀相與
協贊其視舜文五臣四友之助有千載一轍
者豈其神聖獨運哉欽惟

punctuated:
責治於人，有以兼舉而不偏。信乎帝之所以帝，與王之所以王，其率遵是道也已。後之爲治者，不曰「我爲萬乘主，吾固無以桎梏爲也」，則曰「天下固莫巳若，而必自親事也」。故荒淫慆慢者旣以基禍，自作聰明者亦以釀亂，尚奚論哉！

仰惟我太祖高皇帝，獨稟全智，創造區宇，是以虞、周之聖，履虞、周之統也。而其所以因事立法、酌時定制者，綱舉而目張，周慮而曲防，博大詳密，用以綿十萬億無疆之祚。卓乎虞、周之再覩，而聖子神孫所當世守也已！然其所以致此者，則以其功雖無兢，而心恒不自逸；智雖如神，而才恒不自用。故自御曆以來，三十餘年，早朝晏罷，未嘗時刻少怠，信有如聖制之所述矣。然當時名卿碩輔，濟濟布列，有若劉基、宋濂、王禕、陶安若而人，相與諮謀，相與協贊，其視舜、文五臣、四友之助，有千載一轍者，豈其神聖獨運哉！

欽惟陛下，勤政則時御
translation_en:
…demand good governance from others, thereby upholding both principles without partiality. Truly, that by which the Five Emperors reigned as Emperors and the Three Kings ruled as Kings was by consistently following this very Way! Those who governed in later ages, if they did not say, "I am the lord of ten thousand chariots; I certainly have no need to shackle myself with toil," then they said, "No one in the world is my equal, so I must attend to all affairs in person." Thus, those who were dissolute and indolent laid the foundations of disaster, while those who relied on their own cleverness brewed disorder—what more is there to say of them?

Looking up in reverence to our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, i.e., the Hongwu Emperor), he alone was endowed with complete wisdom and founded the realm; thus, with the sageliness of Yu (Shun) and Zhou, he occupied the legitimate succession of Yu and Zhou. The way in which he established laws according to affairs and instituted regulations suited to the times was such that the main principles were upheld and the details extended, with comprehensive foresight and meticulous precautions—vast, great, detailed, and precise—whereby he prolonged a boundless imperial fortune of trillions of years. Eminently, it was the reappearance of Yu and Zhou, and that which his sage sons and divine grandsons ought to guard for generations! Yet the reason he was able to achieve this was that, although his merit was peerless, his mind never indulged in self-ease; although his wisdom was godlike, he never relied solely on his own talent. Therefore, from the time he ascended the throne, for more than thirty years he held court early and retired late, never relaxing even for a moment—truly just as Your Majesty's imperial decree has stated. Yet at that time, renowned ministers and great辅佐 (counselors) were arrayed in dignified multitude—men such as Liu Ji 劉基, Song Lian 宋濂, Wang祎 王禕, and Tao An 陶安—with whom he consulted and planned, and who joined in assisting him. Compared to the aid given to Shun and King Wen by the Five Ministers and the Four Friends, they followed the exact same track across a thousand years; how could it have been merely his divine sageliness operating all alone?

Reverently reflecting upon Your Majesty: in your diligence in governance, you frequently repair to…

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
便殿親與輔臣裁决萬幾勤學則日御
講帷嘉與儒臣討論六籍二帝三王之大經大
法則大書而揭諸
殿廷敬天至節用十二事則懸牌而置之
座右是不自逸之心即舜文之心我
太祖之心也其不自用之心亦即舜文之心我
太祖之心也故纘承基隆之業規恢累洽之治甫
及五載而海內殷富生民樂業以久任責守
宰而吏治興以疆圉責將帥而武威振則其
治亦即虞周之治我
===
太祖之治也臣伏讀
聖制乃猶以帑庾未充民生寡遂吏治之罔宣武
威之靡振而致疑於因循之積弊難驟變久
弛之舊章難遽舉且
諭之曰兹欲革文冒破拘攣使人得其情事循其
理將何如而可此
陛下求治無巳之心即所謂不自逸之心也然世
巳號為極治而猶未免云云乃其弊源
陛下固巳昭徹之矣何也則文冒拘攣是也蓋上
以實責下而下不以實應上此文冒之弊為

以實責下而下不以實應上此文冒之弊爲
punctuated: 便殿，親與輔臣裁决萬幾；勤學則日御講帷，嘉與儒臣討論六籍；二帝三王之大經大法，則大書而揭諸殿廷；敬天至節用十二事，則懸牌而置之座右。是不自逸之心，即舜、文之心，我太祖之心也；其不自用之心，亦即舜、文之心，我太祖之心也。故纘承基隆之業，規恢累洽之治，甫及五載，而海內殷富，生民樂業，以久任責守宰而吏治興，以疆圉責將帥而武威振，則其治亦即虞、周之治，我太祖之治也。臣伏讀聖制，乃猶以帑庾未充、民生寡遂、吏治之罔宣、武威之靡振，而致疑於因循之積弊難驟變，久弛之舊章難遽舉，且諭之曰：「兹欲革文冒，破拘攣，使人得其情，事循其理，將何如而可？」此陛下求治無巳之心，即所謂不自逸之心也。然世巳號為極治，而猶未免云云，乃其弊源，陛下固巳昭徹之矣。何也？則文冒、拘攣是也。蓋上以實責下，而下不以實應上，此文冒之弊為
translation_en:
… the informal palace halls, personally deciding the myriad affairs of state with the grand secretaries; in Your diligence in learning, You daily attend the lecture curtain, delighting in discussing the Six Classics with the Confucian ministers. As for the great principles and fundamental laws of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, You have them written in large characters and displayed in the palace halls; as for the twelve matters from Revering Heaven down to Economizing on Expenditures, You have them inscribed on plaques and placed to the right of Your throne. This mind that does not indulge in ease is the very mind of Shun and King Wen, and the mind of our Grand Progenitor (Taizu); and Your mind that does not rely solely on itself is likewise the very mind of Shun and King Wen, and the mind of our Grand Progenitor. Thus, having succeeded to the enterprise of great prosperity and broadened the governance of cumulative peace, barely five years have passed, yet all within the seas is affluent, the people rejoice in their livelihoods, administrative governance flourishes through holding regional and local officials accountable via long tenure, and military prestige is roused through holding commanders accountable for the frontiers. Your governance, then, is also the very governance of Yu [Shun] and Zhou, and the governance of our Grand Progenitor.

When Your servant humbly reads the Sacred Decree, You nevertheless still express concern that the treasuries and granaries are not yet full, the people's livelihoods are rarely fulfilled, official administration is not diffused, and military prestige is not roused; and You raise doubts as to whether the accumulated abuses of passive routine are difficult to suddenly change, and whether old statutes long relaxed are difficult to abruptly revive. Moreover, You instruct us, saying: "Now, if We wish to eradicate superficiality and falsification, break through rigid adherence to petty rules, cause men to fulfill their true capabilities, and make affairs follow their proper principles, how may this be achieved?" This is Your Majesty's ceaseless mind in seeking good governance—which is precisely what is meant by a mind that does not indulge in ease. Yet when the age is already acclaimed as one of utmost order, and still cannot avoid such concerns as You mention, Your Majesty has in fact already clearly penetrated to the source of these abuses. What is it? It is none other than superficiality and falsification, and rigid adherence to petty rules. For when superiors demand reality from subordinates, yet subordinates do not respond to superiors with reality, this is caused by the abuse of superficiality and falsification …

title: 萬曆五年進士登科錄
text:
之也上以法爲衡而下不以權運法此拘攣
之弊爲之也工炫飾之術則不可以致功守
局曲之見則不可與立業兩弊不去而欲以
爲治不可得也夫惟有忠信貞慤之臣而後
不以欺謾僨事夫惟有明敏任事之臣而後
不以執一隳功由是以理財則制其出入清
其冗濫何患於帑庾之未充以治民則寬其
賦斂軫其疾苦何患於民生之寡遂守宰奉
法循理布上德意以惠元元則所謂吏治之
罔宣無有也將帥講武練兵及時閑暇以備
===
不虞則所謂武備之靡振無有也蓋莫不輸
情以獻忠奉上以守職振作於一時而因循
之積弊頓革修復於俄頃而久弛之舊章頓
舉尚何虞周之治猶未比隆
太祖之成業猶未紹休也哉蓋
陛下有是不自逸之心而又以其心慎擇俊彥旁
羅賢豪推誠以任之覈實以課之無徒取具
故事僅守成迹而務以成精明之治功俊偉
之洪業則
陛下固惟端拱穆清端冕凝旒以聽天下之治舉

之也；上以法爲衡，而下不以權運法，此拘攣之弊爲之也。工炫飾之術，則不可以致功；守局曲之見，則不可與立業。兩弊不去，而欲以爲治，不可得也。夫惟有忠信貞慤之臣，而後不以欺謾僨事；夫惟有明敏任事之臣，而後不以執一隳功。由是以理財，則制其出入、清其冗濫，何患於帑庾之未充？以治民，則寬其賦斂、軫其疾苦，何患於民生之寡遂？守宰奉法循理，布上德意以惠元元，則所謂吏治之罔宣，無有也；將帥講武練兵，及時閑暇以備不虞，則所謂武備之靡振，無有也。蓋莫不輸情以獻忠、奉上以守職，振作於一時而因循之積弊頓革，修復於俄頃而久弛之舊章頓舉。尚何虞、周之治猶未比隆，太祖之成業猶未紹休也哉！
蓋陛下有是不自逸之心，而又以其心慎擇俊彥、旁羅賢豪，推誠以任之，覈實以課之，無徒取具故事、僅守成迹，而務以成精明之治功、俊偉之洪業，則陛下固惟端拱穆清、端冕凝旒，以聽天下之治、舉…
translation_en:
… what brings it about; when the ruler uses the law as a balance scale, yet subordinates do not apply the law with flexibility according to circumstances, this is brought about by the abuse of rigid pedantry. If one is skilled only in the art of showy embellishment, one cannot achieve real results; if one clings to narrow, parochial views, one cannot establish great enterprises with him. If these two abuses are not removed and yet one wishes to achieve good governance, it is impossible to attain. Only when there are ministers who are loyal, trustworthy, upright, and sincere will affairs not be ruined through deception and fraud; only when there are ministers who are discerning, quick-witted, and willing to shoulder responsibilities will achievements not be destroyed through stubborn inflexibility. Proceeding from this, in managing finances, one will regulate revenues and expenditures and clear away superfluous excesses—what worry then that the treasuries and granaries are not full? In governing the people, one will relax their taxes and levies and show compassion for their hardships and sufferings—what worry then that the people's livelihoods are rarely fulfilled? When prefects and magistrates uphold the law and follow principle, spreading the virtuous intentions of the sovereign to benefit the common people, then what was called the failure to propagate civil governance will no longer exist; when generals and commanders study military affairs and drill the troops, taking advantage of times of leisure to prepare for the unexpected, then what was called the failure to invigorate military preparedness will no longer exist. Indeed, all without exception will pour forth their true feelings to offer loyalty and serve their sovereign by keeping to their duties; roused to action all at once, the accumulated abuses of passive routine will suddenly be reformed, and restored in a brief moment, the long-relaxed old statutes will suddenly be revived. How could it still be that the governance of Yu [Shun] and the Zhou is not yet equaled in splendor, or that the established enterprise of the Grand Progenitor (Taizu) is not yet continued in its glory!

Indeed, since Your Majesty possesses this mind that does not indulge in self-ease, if with this very mind You carefully select outstanding talents and widely gather worthy and heroic men, extending sincerity to entrust them with office and verifying realities to evaluate their performance—not merely going through the motions of precedent or merely clinging to established tracks, but striving to accomplish brilliant achievements of governance and a magnificent, grand enterprise—then Your Majesty may truly just sit in dignified repose in the serene heights of the palace, with ceremonial cap straight and jade pendants still, listening to the governance of the empire and raising up…

punctuated: 天下之事，目其難為者，亦豈必其屑屑然為之自已哉？彼□□有為者，則恒勞精瘁神，不免刻厲之過，□不知無逸之主，在於簡以御煩；有見於無為者，則與其臣交習於玩愒，日以因循廢弛，而不知無為之君，必先勞而後逸。故古之聖帝明王，必曰「大有為」，又曰「中心無為，以守至正」。夫無為非縱弛也，是所謂不自逸而亦不自用者也；夫有為非叢脞也，是所謂不自用而用以人者也。有臣以代之為，則王者固可以無為；無為而實無不為，乃所謂大有為也。以其大有為者，廓求治之量，而無一念之自逸；以其無為者，操恭已之術，而無一事之自用，□□臣之所望於陛下者哉！□□無為之說亦精矣。《易》曰：「無思也，無為也，寂然不動，感而遂通天下之故。」而《中庸》亦曰：「喜怒哀樂之未發，謂之中。」故有所倚著，則邪，□□正之本體也。何也？無喜無□□□□之體本如是也；無喜而喜，□□□□為樂，心體之太公順應本如是也。必如是，乃謂之中，乃謂之無為以
translation_en: …among all the affairs of the realm, when viewing those that are difficult to accomplish, why must one fussily undertake them all by oneself? Those who [have insight only into?] active exertion constantly exhaust their vital energy and wear out their spirit, inevitably falling into the excess of harsh severity, [yet] fail to understand that a ruler who does not indulge in ease relies on simplicity to govern complexity. Meanwhile, those who catch sight only of non-action mutually accustom themselves and their ministers to negligence and idling, growing more bound by routine and laxity day by day, while failing to understand that a ruler who practices non-action must first labor before enjoying ease. Therefore, of the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity, it was必ず said that they "achieved great things through active exertion," and it was also said that "within the mind there is non-action, so as to preserve supreme rectitude." Now, non-action is not laxity; it is what is meant by neither indulging oneself in ease nor relying solely on one's own personal efforts. And active exertion is not petty meddling; it is what is meant by not relying on one's own efforts alone, but rather employing others to act. When there are ministers to act on his behalf, the true king can indeed practice non-action; practicing non-action while in reality leaving nothing undone is precisely what is called achieving great things through active exertion. Through great active exertion, to broaden the capacity for seeking good governance without a single thought of self-indulgent ease; through non-action, to grasp the art of reverent self-restraint without a single matter handled through self-willed effort—[is this not?] what your servant hopes for from Your Majesty! [Yet?] the doctrine of non-action is also subtle indeed. The Book of Changes (Yi) states: "Without thought, without action, still and unmoving, yet when stimulated it penetrates all the causes of the world." And the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) likewise states: "While pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy are not yet aroused, this is called equilibrium (zhong)." Thus, if there is any partial attachment, it becomes deviant, [and is not?] the original substance of rectitude. Why is this? Having neither pleasure nor [anger, sorrow, or joy—the mind's?] substance is originally like this; having no partial pleasure and yet feeling pleasure, […?] as joy—the supreme impartiality and natural responsiveness of the mind's substance are originally like this. Only when it is like this can it be called equilibrium, and can it be called practicing non-action so as to…
